entries.title: what the residual add and RMSNorm are
entries.text: Each token goes through the model as one vector of 2,048 numbers, its hidden state. Attention reads it and works out a change, and that change is added back on; then the MLP does the same. The running sum is called the residual stream, and the add that writes into it is the residual add. RMSNorm stands for root mean square normalization. The root mean square of a vector is the square root of the average of its squares: one number for how big its values are. Divide the vector by it, with a small ε added under the root so a row of zeros never divides by zero, and what is left has a root mean square of 1; a learned weight per channel then sets the size of each channel. It is a simpler LayerNorm that skips subtracting the mean. The stream itself is never normalized, and every add can make it bigger. So each block reads a normalized copy instead, values of a steady size whatever the stream has grown to. That is why the two come as a pair: the sum one block writes is the very row the next block's norm reads. TinyLlama has a norm before each of its 44 attention and MLP blocks, and an add after each.

entries.title: every add is followed by a norm
entries.text: A transformer layer never replaces its input; it adds to it. After attention, and again after the MLP, the layer's output is added to the residual stream, and that sum is what the next block reads. The next block first normalizes it with RMSNorm: divide the row by the root of its mean square, then scale by a learned weight per dimension. So every add is followed by a norm of the same row.

entries.title: fusion keeps the value on the chip
entries.text: Every separate elementwise kernel reads its inputs from DRAM, does a little arithmetic, writes its output back and pays a launch. Two in a row send the value between them out to DRAM and read it straight back. Fusing the two keeps that value in registers. The bytes of the round trip and one launch disappear, and the arithmetic is the same. At decode the math was never the cost, so what fusion saves is bytes and the gap before a launch, not arithmetic. Here the fused kernel moves about 8.4 KB per token where the pair moves more (calculated from the bytes per launch), and a decode step runs fewer kernels (measured). Fewer bytes still did not make the first fused kernel faster: at one token it took about the same time as the pair. The errata entry "Fusing two kernels saved bytes, not time" tells that story. The same pattern returns in SwiGLU, chapter 11. CUDA Graphs, a later chapter, remove the launch part of the cost for every kernel at once.

entries.title: the pair sends the sum out and back
entries.text: The naive version runs them as two kernels. add writes the sum to memory; rmsnorm then reads it back, twice, once for the squares and once to scale it. A fused kernel reads x, the residual and the weight once, writes the sum and the norm once, and keeps the sum on the chip in between. The DRAM traffic falls to about 540 KB per launch, and one launch replaces two.

entries.title: fewer bytes did not buy time
entries.text: The first fused kernel runs one block of 256 threads per row. Each thread adds and squares a few values, the block reduces the squares, one thread computes rstd and shares it, and a second pass reads the sums back and writes the norm. It moves a third fewer bytes, but takes the same time as the pair: about 12 µs for one token. The memory traffic is a small part of that; the rest is waiting on dependent loads and barriers. So the bytes fusion saves turn into time only once the kernel stops waiting on itself. The time came later, from cutting those waits: 16-byte loads, the sums kept in registers, and one barrier instead of two.

entries.title: round to BF16 where the pair rounds
entries.text: The spec asks for a sum bit-identical to the naive add, and a norm equal to the naive RMSNorm except for the order the squares are added in. That pins down where every rounding to BF16 happens. Two review fixes came from it: square the sum after rounding it, since the naive kernel only ever sees the rounded value, and round the normalized value before multiplying by the weight, as the naive kernel does.

entries.title: 16 bytes per load, not 2
entries.text: A row is split into pieces of 16 bytes, one per thread. The tuned kernel loads each piece with one 128-bit instruction instead of a separate small load for every value, for x and the residual alike. It also keeps the rounded sums in registers, so the second pass never goes back to memory for them, and writes the sum and the norm with 128-bit stores.

entries.title: shuffles give every thread the total
entries.text: Adding up the squares used to end with the total in one thread, which then shared rstd through shared memory behind a second barrier. With xor shuffles, each lane swaps partial sums with the lane whose index differs in one bit. After a few swaps all the lanes of a warp hold the warp's total; after one barrier and one more round over the warps, every thread holds the row's total and computes rstd itself.

entries.title: 3.0x faster than the pair, one token
entries.text: The tuned kernel takes 4 µs for one token, about a third of the pair's time, and stays near that up to the largest token count measured. Try the token counts on the right. In a decode step, the add + RMSNorm launches are now about 1% of the time. The gain only became real once the kernel was faster than the pair it replaced, not just one launch fewer. On Llama 3 8B a row has 4,096 values instead of 2,048, in 32 layers instead of 22, so these launches move about 2.9 times the bytes per token, while the weights a step reads grow about 7.3 times, from about 2.1 GB to about 15 GB: their share of the bytes falls. Their time here is set more by waits than by bytes, and nothing was measured on an H100; the numbers are calculated from published specs.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: Every separate elementwise kernel reads its inputs from DRAM, writes its output back and pays a launch. Fusing two neighbours keeps the value between them in registers, so that round trip and one launch disappear. SwiGLU (chapter 11) uses the pattern again, and CUDA Graphs (chapter 13) remove the launch cost for every kernel. Matching the naive pair means preserving where values round to BF16. The norm must use the rounded sum, and its result must round before the learned weight is applied. Fewer bytes alone do not guarantee less time. The first fused kernel waited on dependent loads and barriers and ran as long as the pair. Wide loads fetch several values per instruction, registers keep the rounded sums for reuse, and xor shuffles let every thread compute the scale; these removed those waits.

entries.title: what an online softmax is
entries.text: Attention decides how much each earlier token matters to the one being generated. Each query head takes the dot product of its query with the key of every token in the context, 64 values each, and divides it by the square root of that size. That gives one score per token, and a score can be any number. Softmax turns the scores into weights that are positive and add up to 1. Each weight is e to the power of its score minus m, divided by l: m is the largest score, and l is the sum of those powers over every score. Subtracting m does not change the weights, but it keeps every power small, so none can overflow. The weights then say how much of each token's value vector goes into the head's output. On a GPU this is awkward: no weight is known until m and l are, and both depend on every score, the last one included. The direct way keeps every score and reads them several times. An online softmax reads the scores once and keeps m and l as running values. A score below m just adds its term to l. A larger score becomes the new m, and l is first multiplied by e to the power of the old m minus the new one, which measures the old terms against the new maximum. After the last score, m and l are exactly right, and the same trick works for the weighted sum of the values.

entries.title: one pass: a running max, sum and output
entries.text: v2 reads the keys in chunks of 256 and keeps three things between chunks: the largest score so far, the sum of exponentials, and the weighted values. When a chunk brings a larger score, the old sum and values are scaled down by exp(m_old − m_new) and the new chunk is added. The result is the same softmax, in one pass, and shared memory holds one chunk: 3,456 bytes at any length. With no buffer of scores, nothing in the kernel caps the context.

entries.title: eight lanes share each key in one wide read
entries.text: A score is a dot product over 64 values. If each thread computes a whole one alone, neighbouring threads read keys a whole key apart. In v2 a group of 8 lanes shares one key: at every step they read neighbouring dimensions together, in one wide read, and a few shuffles add their partial sums. The values step also uses every thread, where one thread per dimension would leave most of the block waiting.

entries.title: faster from busier warps, not more bandwidth
entries.text: Nsight Compute on v2 and on v1, the three-pass kernel it replaced, shows both reading far less than the memory system could deliver, so the gain is not bandwidth. v2 keeps more warps busy and gives them less to wait on. One thing that did not help: replacing v2's shared-memory reductions with warp shuffles was 15 to 20% slower, so it was dropped.

entries.title: v1 kept every score and passed three times
entries.text: v1, the first version, gives each row and query head one thread block. Pass one writes a score for every token of the context into shared memory. Pass two finds the maximum, then the exponentials and their sum. Pass three multiplies by the values, one thread per dimension: only 64 of the block's threads work and the rest wait. Each thread also computes a whole dot product alone. One row at a long context: about 600 µs.

entries.title: keeping every score capped the context
entries.text: Keeping every score means shared memory grows with the context, one float per token. The host code sizes it from the block table and refuses any table longer than 2,048 tokens, TinyLlama's full context. That is why the longest rows of the benchmark read n/a for v1. The memory itself was not the wall: at the cap v1 uses 9,344 bytes per block, a fifth of the default limit. The cap was a design choice that a longer model would have hit, and the online softmax removed it.

entries.title: in the decode step, the gain grows with the batch
entries.text: Wired into the runner, attention per decode step fell to about 270 µs on short contexts. The figure shows v1's time beside it. Batch 16 gained the most, because attention work grows with the number of rows while the weight reads of the GEMVs do not.

entries.title: faster at every size, least at the shortest
entries.text: From a context of a few hundred tokens up v2 is about 3x faster than v1; at the shortest context with one row there is little to overlap and the gain is smaller. Try the measured times on the right. With a single row v2 still launches only 32 blocks, one per query head. The chapter split attention cuts the context to fill the rest of the GPU.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: An online softmax keeps a running maximum and sum and rescales them whenever a chunk brings a larger score. That makes it one pass, and shared memory holds one chunk, 3,456 bytes at any context length, instead of growing with the context. Neither kernel came near the memory limit, with DRAM throughput at most 6.4%. The win came from keeping more warps busy and letting a group of lanes share a key so its loads sit side by side. A much faster kernel does not make the whole step much faster. Attention was a small slice of a batch-1 step, which gained only about 5.5% in tokens per second.

entries.title: what prefill, decode and a chunk are
entries.text: A request is answered in two phases. Prefill runs every token of the prompt through the model in one forward pass: all 22 layers see all the positions together, each layer writes their keys and values into the KV cache, and the logits of the last position give the first output token. The wait for it is the time to first token, TTFT. Decode follows. Each step feeds the newest token back in as a single row, reads the keys and values already in the cache instead of computing them again, and produces the next token. A decoding request moves exactly one token per step, so the time between its tokens is the length of a step. The engine serves many requests at once, and a step is one forward pass over all their rows together: one row for each decoding request, and one for each prompt token in prefill. A step costs more the more rows it has, and nobody gets a token until it ends, so a step that holds a long prompt makes every decoding request wait for that whole prefill. Chunked prefill cuts the prompt into pieces. Each step gets a token budget, a cap on its rows: the decode rows go in first and a chunk of the prompt fills what is left. The prompt fills its cache over several steps, and no step grows past the budget, so the decoders keep their pace. The rest of this chapter is how the engine's scheduler picks those rows.

entries.title: one prompt stops everyone
entries.text: The scheduler of chapter 17 makes every step all prefill or all decode, and prefill goes first. A long prompt is one step, and every running sequence waits for it: alone, the long prompt takes about 160 ms. Measured under Poisson arrivals, the longest wait between two tokens of one request is about 110 ms with whole-prompt steps, many times the median gap. The FlashAttention prefill kernel of Part II already shortened that step: with per-row prefill attention the same prompt took about 1.2 s. Every load number in this chapter is measured with the new kernel.

entries.title: a step is a token budget
entries.text: schedule_chunked(token_budget) caps the rows of a step. Every sequence whose prefill is done gets its decode row first. What is left goes to the one sequence still in prefill, as a chunk that starts where it stopped. Only if budget remains is the next waiting request admitted, first come, first served. A step never exceeds the budget, and a budget below max_batch is refused.

entries.title: the budget trades the prompt's wait for everyone's
entries.text: The prompt takes as many steps as its chunks need, and the decoders keep their row in each. A smaller budget means more steps, so the prompt's first token comes later: the budget trades the prompt's wait against everyone else's. Measured with a long prompt arriving among decoding requests, a budget cuts the longest gap to 38 ms, and the prompt's first token comes later. Under load the same budget raises peak goodput to about 4.5 requests per second, still below vLLM, so the stalls were only part of the gap. Pick a budget on the right; the prompt and the decoders there are an example, not a benchmark.

entries.title: preemption takes the prompt first
entries.text: The preemption rule of chapter 17 does not change: when a decoder needs a block and none is free, the victim is the back of the running list. What changes is who stands there. Blocks for the whole prompt are allocated at admission, so a sequence in prefill never runs out halfway, but it can be taken from. The sequence in prefill is always last, so partly prefilled work goes first. It returns to the front of the waiting queue and starts again at position 0.

entries.title: only finished chunks get logits
entries.text: The sampled list holds every decode row, then each sequence whose chunk reaches the end of its length. A chunk that stops short has no entry and no logits. update() takes exactly one token per sampled entry, in that order. It can be empty, and the call is still required. first_token is stamped when the token arrives, not at the first chunk. This list is what the runner was wired to. The spec came first, with 25 tests that 14 deliberately broken schedulers fail. Joe implemented it, and one fix drafted with Claude followed: a preempted decoder now replays its prompt and its output. The batch builder then put the decode rows first and the chunk rows after them, with logit rows only for the sampled sequences. Pure decode steps kept their CUDA Graph, and a step that holds a chunk runs without one.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: A token budget of 256 caps all rows in a step. Decode rows go first and the prompt fills what is left. A smaller budget spreads a long prompt over more steps, delaying its first token while shortening the waits for running requests. When cache space runs out, the partly prefilled sequence is preempted first. Its progress is lost and it starts again when admitted.

entries.title: what a CUDA Graph is
entries.text: Everything in the chapters so far runs on the GPU as kernels. A kernel is one function written for the GPU and run there by thousands of threads at once: a GEMV, RoPE, attention and a norm are each a kernel. CUDA is NVIDIA's platform for writing and running them; the name was first spelled out as Compute Unified Device Architecture. The engine's own C++ runs on the CPU, and the CPU decides which kernel comes next. The GPU does not start a kernel on its own. The CPU asks for each one with a kernel launch: which function, how many thread blocks, which arguments. The request costs the CPU microseconds of work in the CUDA driver and goes onto a stream, a queue the GPU works through in order. A kernel begins only when the one before it has finished and the GPU has set up the next one, so there is a short gap before every kernel. Next to a long kernel the gap is nothing; next to a short one it can take as long as the kernel. A CUDA Graph hands the GPU the same work another way. The chain of launches is written down once as a graph: every kernel is a node that keeps its function, its grid and its arguments, with an edge from the kernel that has to run before it. From then on the whole chain goes to the GPU with a single launch, and the GPU moves from one kernel to the next with almost no gap. A decode step is such a chain, hundreds of kernels in a fixed order, and the rest of this chapter measures what its gaps cost and what it takes to record it.

entries.title: the CPU keeps up, the GPU still idles
entries.text: A decode step of TinyLlama is 224 kernels: the same kernels in every layer, plus the embedding, the last norm and the LM head. Run eagerly, the CPU hands each one to the GPU with its own cudaLaunchKernel, which costs the CPU a dozen or so microseconds under the profiler. The launches queue up on a stream and the GPU runs them in order. The CPU keeps up easily: in the middle of a step it is well ahead, launching kernels several layers further on. And still the GPU is idle for about 15% of the step.

entries.title: a gap before every kernel adds up
entries.text: Zoomed in, the idle time is a few microseconds before every kernel. Between two kernels launched one by one on a stream, the GPU lets the first finish completely, then takes the next launch from the queue and sets up its grid before its first block runs. The median gap is about 3.1 µs, whatever the CPU is doing. A few microseconds is nothing next to a long gate/up GEMV, but a step has hundreds of these boundaries, and several of the kernels in a layer run for only a few microseconds. Together they come to about 1,200 µs per step. Faster kernels would not touch it; fewer launches would.

entries.title: record the step once, launch it as one
entries.text: A CUDA Graph is the whole sequence of launches recorded once and handed to the GPU as one unit. DecodeGraphs records it with stream capture: between cudaStreamBeginCapture and cudaStreamEndCapture, the kernels that run_staged launches are not run but added to a graph, each one after the one before it. Instantiating the graph checks it and prepares it for launch, once, at startup. From then on a decode step is one cudaGraphLaunch. Capture has rules: nothing may allocate memory or wait for the GPU, which is why every graph is captured right after one eager run of the same step, when cuBLAS has already picked and loaded its kernels; its workspace is memory the engine gave it up front.

entries.title: same addresses, new values
entries.text: A graph stores each kernel with the arguments it was captured with: the same pointers, the same grid. A replay cannot be told "these are this step's tokens". So the step's inputs go where the graph already looks: stage copies the token ids, positions, KV slots, context lengths and block tables into one buffer of the runner, outside the graph, and the captured kernels read them there. The arrays sit at offsets that depend on the number of rows, and so does every GEMM's shape. A batch is padded up to the next bucket with rows that write nowhere and attend to nothing, so it replays that bucket's graph. Together 8 buckets cover every decode batch up to 16 rows.

entries.title: a replay cuts the gaps, not the kernels
entries.text: Switch the step on the right: the same kernels, from the two profiles, close up. The median gap drops to 0.24 µs, and the GPU is idle for far less of the step. The kernels themselves take the same time. Without the profiler the saving is 0.85 ms per token at batch 1 and about 1.2 ms at 16: roughly a fixed amount per step, since every step has the same boundaries. It is a bigger share of a token from a lone request than of a token in a full batch. Prefill steps are not graphed. Llama 3 8B on an H100 runs the same kernels in each of 32 layers instead of 22, about 1.5 times the boundaries, while reading its weights takes about 4.5 ms there against about 6.4 ms here, since the H100 reads memory about 10 times faster. If the gaps were as long there, they would be a larger share of the step, not a smaller one. The floors are calculated from published specs; launch gaps on an H100 were not measured.

entries.title: finer buckets pad fewer rows
entries.text: The padded rows that let a batch replay a bucket's graph write nothing, but they are not free: every kernel in the graph runs at the bucket's row count, padding included. With one bucket per power of two, a batch of 17 rows replays the 32-row graph, and 15 of the rows it pays for are padding. So decode_graph_buckets adds sizes in between: it walks from each power of two to the next in equal steps, 2 of them by default, and ends at the max batch. The same batch now replays the 24-row graph. Padding it to 32 rows instead costs 14% more time per token (calculated from the two measured runs). Finer steps gained nothing more, so the default stays at 2.

entries.title: the frozen grid froze the split count
entries.text: The frozen grid caught up with the engine once. Split attention cuts a long context across several thread blocks per head, and the split count is part of the attention kernel's grid. The graphs were captured on an empty dummy batch, so every replay ran the one-split kernel: at a long prompt eager became faster than the graphs. Now the constructor walks the contexts up to the longest it serves and captures again whenever a bucket's split count changes, so there are more graphs. A replay picks its graph from the batch's longest context, and at a long prompt the time per token falls to about 9.1 ms.

entries.title: past 64 rows, more rows buy little
entries.text: Every number so far stops at 16 rows. Raise the max batch, submit twice that many requests at once, and the throughput with graphs keeps climbing up to 64 rows: about 2,800 tok/s (measured). After that it nearly stops: 4 times the rows add little. Two things change there. Attention reads each row's own keys and values, so its time grows with the rows, and by 128 rows it is 50% of the step. And the GEMMs of chapter 3 stop being one read of the weights that every row shares: past the ridge they are compute bound, and their time grows with the rows too. From then on a step with twice the rows takes about twice as long, and a bigger batch buys almost nothing.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: Launched one by one, every kernel is preceded by a gap of a few microseconds while the GPU takes the next launch and sets up its grid. Those gaps leave the GPU idle for about 15% of a batch-1 decode step, and faster kernels would not remove them. A CUDA Graph records the chain of launches once and replays it with a single launch, which cuts the idle share to 1.4% while the kernels take the same time. The saving is about a fixed time per step, because every step has the same kernel boundaries. A graph freezes each kernel's pointers and grid, so a replay can only change values. Inputs go through fixed buffers, and anything that changes a grid, like the split count of attention, needs its own graph. Batches are padded to a bucket, and padded rows are still computed, so the buckets come 2 per power of two: padding 17 rows to 32 instead of 24 costs about 14% more time per token.

entries.title: what FlashAttention is
entries.text: Prefill computes attention for every token of a prompt at once. Each token is a query row, and row t scores itself against the keys of tokens 0 to t. Laid out as a table, query rows down and keys across, the scores fill a triangle, and the triangle grows with the square of the prompt. The direct way computes the whole table, stores it, runs a softmax along every row and then multiplies by the values. For a long prompt the table is far larger than anything that fits on the chip, so it goes out to DRAM and comes back. FlashAttention cuts the table into tiles: a block of query rows against a block of keys. One tile of scores is computed, used and dropped while it is still on the chip. The online softmax of the attention v1 to v2 chapter is what allows it: every query row keeps a running maximum, a running sum and a running weighted sum of the values, and rescales them when a later tile brings a larger score. Two things follow. A tile of keys and values is loaded once for a whole block of query rows instead of once per row. And a tile of queries times a tile of keys is a small matrix multiply, the shape the tensor cores are built for.

entries.title: prefill is a square of rows against keys
entries.text: Prefill attention scores every prompt token against every token before it: t query rows, each against up to t keys. Twice the prompt is twice the rows, each with twice the keys, so the products grow with the square of the length. The keys and values themselves are small, 2.1 MB per layer at 2,048 tokens. Nearly all of the cost is arithmetic, and that belongs on the tensor cores. The engine first ran it as decode does: one row per prompt token, one thread block per row and query head, and row t walks its whole context of t + 1 keys and values alone. Every key is fetched again by every row after it, and none of that work uses the tensor cores. At 2,048 tokens the engine took 6.4 times as long as llama.cpp, calculated from the two times measured in one session.

entries.title: sixteen rows share each key tile
entries.text: The way out is to change who walks. One warp owns 16 query rows of one head and loads them once. The keys of the sequence then stream past in tiles of the same size, and every row of the query tile uses each key tile. A row must still see only its own past. Keys after a query are masked, and keys past the last row of the tile load as zeros, so no row depends on what follows it. Keys the sequence already has in the KV cache come through the block table, and the chunk's own come from the QKV buffer. A chunk is the run of prompt rows one step prefills: the whole prompt, unless the scheduler of Part IV splits it.

entries.title: a tile of scores is a small matrix multiply
entries.text: The scores of a tile are a small matrix multiply, and the tensor cores have an instruction for exactly that, mma.sync. One call takes 16 query rows by 16 dimensions and 16 dimensions by 8 keys, and adds their product to 16 × 8 scores kept in FP32. The operands are fragments: every lane of the warp holds a fixed few elements of each matrix in its own registers. A key tile goes through as two halves of 8 keys, and a head of 64 dimensions takes 4 calls per half.

entries.title: a softmax per row keeps it all in registers
entries.text: After the two halves, a lane holds the scores of its two query rows against four keys. That is exactly what the next product, weights times values, wants from that lane as its first operand. So the scores turn into weights where they are, and nothing is passed between lanes to set it up. In between sits the online softmax, once per row. Each score is rounded as in the other attention kernels and masked, then the row's maximum and sum are reduced over the 4 lanes that share the row, with two shuffles. The weights are rounded to BF16 and multiplied with the values through the same instruction. A row carries only its maximum, its sum and its weighted values from one key tile to the next, and the lanes that hold the row keep them in registers. The scores of a tile are used and dropped, so the kernel needs no shared memory and no barrier.

entries.title: tests pin what a faster kernel could break
entries.text: Before any kernel there was a written spec and 24 tests. The spec fixes the interface: one call handles every prefill chunk of a step. chunk_starts says which rows belong to which chunk, cached_lens how many tokens of that sequence are already in the KV cache, and there is one block table row per chunk instead of one per token. The tests pin what a faster kernel could break without anyone noticing. A row must not depend on the rows after it or on what else is in the call, bit for bit. And the kernel must not read cache slots outside its context, which the tests fill with NaN.

entries.title: a shorter path to each byte, the same walk
entries.text: The first kernel used what the interface offered: it read the chunk's own keys and values straight from the QKV buffer instead of going through the cache, and it kept an online softmax. It also kept the shape of the decode kernels: one thread block per row and head, one key at a time, two barriers per key. Every test passed. Wired into the runner and measured, it was slower than the path it replaced: about 1,600 ms at 2,048 tokens. Moving where the bytes come from saves nothing when every row still walks every key alone. The tiled kernel came next and passed the same tests unchanged.

entries.title: a 16 by 16 tile is what a warp's registers hold
entries.text: The weighted values add up in FP32 and are scaled down when a row's maximum rises. A lane keeps 32 of those accumulators in registers, next to its piece of the query tile. That sets the tile size: 16 by 16 is what one warp can hold in registers at a head of 64 dimensions, and what one mma shape gives without moving data between lanes. Warps share nothing. Two details keep it that way. The value columns are interleaved, so the values a lane needs from one key sit side by side and load as whole words. And the kernel is a template on the head size, so its loops unroll and its arrays stay in registers.

entries.title: registers decide how many blocks run at once
entries.text: The same registers limit how many thread blocks an SM can run. The kernel first needed 115 per thread, so 4 blocks fit on an SM and 104 on the GPU. Under a token budget of 256, chunked prefill sends a prompt 256 rows at a time, and a 256-row chunk launches 128 blocks. The last 24 waited and then ran on a nearly empty GPU. Chunking a lone 2,048-token prompt cost 24%, most of it in this kernel. Two divisions on the path that finds a cached key were done in 64 bits. In 32 bits the compiler needs 96 registers, 130 blocks fit and a chunk's 128 run together. The split now costs 14%. The step has moved, not gone: at a budget of 272 a chunk launches 136 blocks, and they take about 71 ms of attention where 128 take about 51.

entries.title: the square stays, the cost per token goes flat
entries.text: As the default, the tiled kernel takes one 2,048-token prompt to its first token in about 160 ms. The figure puts the per-row path, the first kernel and llama.cpp from the same session beside it. The work still grows with the square of the prompt: the kernel computes the same number of score and value products. But each key tile is read once per 16 rows and the products run on the tensor cores, and the cost per prompt token stays flat, at most 0.086 ms.

entries.title: the gain is largest where the square was
entries.text: The gain is largest where the square was largest, 7.2 times less time at 2,048 tokens, and it shrinks with the prompt. Pick a length on the right to see the four measured paths. llama.cpp's number is the time of its prompt decode calls with no sampler, and the engine's includes sampling the first token, so the two are not timed in quite the same way. The engine is ahead at every length measured.

entries.title: your turn: 8 heads read the same keys
entries.text: TinyLlama has 32 query heads and 4 KV heads, so 8 query heads use the same keys and values. The kernel gives every query head its own warp, 4 to a thread block, and each warp loads every key and value tile for itself. Nsight Compute counts the loads asking the caches for about 3,300 MB per layer, to use 2.1 MB of keys and values. Count it the way the roofline does. A value is 2 bytes, and every query row that uses it does one multiply and one add, so a load is worth 1 FLOP per byte for each row that shares it: 16 FLOP per byte with 16 rows to a warp. Now let one thread block serve all 8 query heads of a KV head and load each tile once. Where does the kernel land against the ridge, 107 FLOP per byte on this GPU? Commit to an answer on the right, then work it out. Know what the answer can say. It counts bytes loaded, not bytes from DRAM: about 94% of today's loads are already in L1, and DRAM runs at 1.3% of its throughput. The tensor cores run at about 20% of their peak rate, and what holds them is registers: 96 per thread fill 39% of the warp places, and at that count a block of 8 warps would fit 2 to an SM, 16 warps where 20 run today (calculated). The loads that sharing removes are cache traffic, and whether that traffic holds the kernel back is not measured. Nobody has built it, so the time it saves is not measured either. That is the exercise. Also not measured: the stall reasons per source line, and more or fewer warps per block. The load sweeps of the chunked prefill chapter were rerun with this kernel.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: With one walk per row, a 2,048-token prompt reads 2,098,176 key rows per head; with one pass per 16 rows it reads 132,096 (calculated). The score and value products are the same number, and they move to the tensor cores. Tests prove a kernel right, not fast. The first kernel passed all 24 tests and took about 1,600 ms where the path it replaced took about 1,500 ms (measured), so it stayed behind a switch. The tiled kernel takes the same prompt from about 1,200 to about 160 ms (measured) and keeps the cost per prompt token between 0.074 and 0.086 ms. Nsight Compute, run later, found the tensor cores at about 20% of their peak rate and DRAM at 1.3% of its throughput (measured): neither is at its limit. Registers cap how many warps fit on an SM (measured); whether that is what holds the tensor cores back was not measured.

entries.title: what an inference engine does
entries.text: An inference engine is the program that runs a trained language model: it loads the weights onto the GPU, takes a prompt and writes the answer one token at a time. This one runs TinyLlama, whose 1.1 billion weights are stored in BF16. A token is a word or a piece of one, numbered by its place in a fixed vocabulary: asked “What is the capital of Canada?”, TinyLlama answered “The capital of Canada is Ottawa.” in a few tokens and a stop token. The prompt goes through the model once, all its tokens together. After that every new token costs one decode step. The id of the last token picks one row of the embedding table, 2,048 numbers that stand for that token. The row passes through every layer in turn, and each layer adds to it what attention reads from the earlier tokens and what its MLP computes. At the end the LM head, a matrix with one row for each token of the vocabulary, turns those numbers into one score per token, called logits. One token is picked from them, and its id is the input of the next step. Each of those pieces is one or more GPU kernels, programs the CPU hands to the GPU to run. In the profile a decode step is 224 kernels, some in every layer and a few around them, and one more picks the token; the whole step takes only a few milliseconds on this GPU. The rest of the book takes those kernels one chapter at a time. This chapter starts underneath them all: how a GPU runs a kernel, where its data lives, and why a decode step waits on memory and not on arithmetic.

entries.title: decode waits on memory
entries.text: To produce one token, the GPU has to read every weight of the model once: all the layers, then the LM head. For TinyLlama that is about 2.1 GB. At the bandwidth this GPU's memory can deliver, the reading alone takes several milliseconds. The arithmetic on those weights would take a small fraction of a millisecond if the numbers were already there. So the measured step, about 6.9 ms, is almost all waiting for bytes. Making the maths faster would change nothing; moving fewer bytes, or using each byte for more work, is what helps. Chapter 1 timed its token at about 8.7 ms. That step was launched kernel by kernel while a profiler recorded it; this one is replayed from a CUDA graph, with no profiler. Chapter 13, CUDA Graphs, is about the difference. The rest of this chapter builds this into the roofline, and every later chapter is judged against it.

entries.title: the KV cache remembers
entries.text: Attention lets the newest token look back at every earlier one. Each token gets a query, what it is looking for, a key, what it offers, and a value, what it passes on. The new token compares its query with the key of every earlier token and mixes their values by how well they match. The keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so the engine keeps them: the KV cache. Each step then computes K and V only for the new token and reads the rest, instead of recomputing all of them. The figure counts the computations over eight steps, and the gap grows with every token. The price is memory: 22,528 bytes for every token of every conversation. The paged KV cache and attention chapters are about storing and reading this cache well.

entries.title: batching shares the read
entries.text: If reading the weights is the cost, read them once and use them for many requests. A batch of 16 conversations runs as one step: the weights stream in once, and each row does its own arithmetic on them. The step gets only a little longer, because the arithmetic was nearly free. The output rises to about 1,700 tokens per second, many times what one request gets. This is why serving engines batch everything they can, and why the scheduler of chapter 17, how many requests fit, exists.

entries.title: memory is the budget
entries.text: The weights take a share of the GPU's memory, and most of the rest becomes the KV cache: a pool of about 210,000 token slots. How many conversations fit at once is decided by that pool, not by the arithmetic. Reserving the longest possible answer for each request would fit far fewer of them, most of each reservation empty. Handing out small blocks only as a conversation grows fits about 990 chats of a short length. That is the paged KV cache.

entries.title: batching trades latency for throughput
entries.text: Bigger batches give more tokens per second in total, but each conversation waits a little longer for its next token, about 8.2 ms in a full batch. An engine is always trading the speed one user feels against how many users it can serve. A long new prompt makes the trade worse. Its prefill is one big step, and every conversation already decoding waits for it to finish. Chunked prefill, in Part IV, cuts the prompt into pieces that ride along with the decode steps, so nobody stalls. CUDA Graphs shave the time between kernels so every step is shorter.

entries.title: threads in blocks, warps in lockstep
entries.text: A CUDA kernel is one function that thousands of threads run at once, each on its own piece of the data. One launch is a grid. The grid is cut into blocks, every block has the same number of threads, and a block runs on one streaming multiprocessor (SM) from start to finish. This GPU has 26 SMs. Inside a block the hardware groups threads in warps of 32. A warp executes one instruction at a time for all its threads, so a thread that wants a different branch than its neighbors makes the warp run both. SwiGLU's first draft launched the grid in the figure for every row, with several warps in each block.

entries.title: the nearer the data, the faster
entries.text: A thread can work on data in four places. Global memory is the DRAM that holds the weights and the KV cache; its measured bandwidth on this GPU is about 320 GB/s. On a laptop GPU it is GDDR, not HBM, but the role is the same. The L2 cache sits in front of it and every SM shares it. Each SM also has 100 KB of shared memory, a scratchpad for the threads of a block, and a register file split among its threads. The caption gives the totals over all the SMs. Each step closer to the thread is faster, measured on this GPU: a load waits about 310 ns from DRAM, less from L2 and least from shared memory, and an FMA's result feeds the next after only a few cycles. L2 streams several times what DRAM does, and shared memory moves about twice as much with wide vector loads as with plain word loads.

entries.title: the slower of bytes and FLOPs wins
entries.text: Every operation has to move some bytes from memory and do some arithmetic, and it takes as long as the slower of the two. Take one layer's gate/up projection, a large BF16 matrix. Reading its weights at the measured bandwidth takes about 140 µs (calculated), however many tokens use them. Decoding one token is a matrix times a vector: one FLOP for every byte of weight. At the measured compute peak the arithmetic needs only about 1.3 µs and the GPU waits on memory: memory bound. A long prefill uses each weight once for every prompt token, needs far more arithmetic and waits on nothing but the math: compute bound.

entries.title: the ridge splits memory from compute
entries.text: A roofline plots speed against FLOPs per byte. Its slope is the memory bandwidth and its flat top the compute peak, and they meet at the ridge, about 110 FLOP/byte on this GPU (the compute peak divided by the bandwidth). Left of the ridge an operation is memory bound, right of it compute bound. The bandwidth roof is not a law of physics. It is the 320 GB/s or so that a plain kernel adding two large arrays into a third reached in a bandwidth test on this GPU, some way below the memory's rated speed, so a kernel that streams its bytes a little better can read above 100% of it. Rows that share one read of the weights set the position: FLOP/byte is about the number of rows. The ring climbs the slope as the batch grows and flattens at the ridge. The dots are measured: gate/up at the two smallest row counts, on the slope.

entries.title: decode sits on the slope
entries.text: At a batch of one, the five matrix-vector products of a decode step run at about the bandwidth roof, and the whole step with CUDA Graphs at 93%. Nothing in a decode step is near the ridge, so a faster multiply would not make a token faster: moving fewer bytes would. That is the memory wall. Try the row counts on the right: the memory time never changes, and the compute time only overtakes it past the ridge. Only the two smallest row counts were measured; the others come from the two ceilings.

entries.title: fused kernels skip a trip to memory
entries.text: Each separate kernel starts by reading its inputs from global memory and ends by writing its outputs back, so two kernels in a row pay for the data between them twice. Fusing them keeps that intermediate in registers or shared memory. For add + RMSNorm that is the sum: the naive pair writes it and reads it back twice, the fused kernel does not, and the DRAM traffic falls to about 540 KB, about two thirds of the unfused pair's. The kernel stories that follow are this idea at work, each on one small operation of a layer: add + RMSNorm fuses two kernels into one, SwiGLU moves the gate/up row once with wide vector loads, and RoPE touches only the Q and K slices. Each is under 2% of a decode step; the step is mostly the GEMVs, already at the roof.

entries.title: speed up only what the step waits on
entries.text: The same reading explains a result that looks odd at first. Before the first layer, the embedding lookup copies one row of the embedding table for every token, 2,048 BF16 values, with no arithmetic at all. The first version gave every token its own block, and each thread copied its values one at a time. The fast one, written by Claude at Joe's request, runs over all the rows at once and gives each thread 8 values in a single 16-byte load. Its output is bit-identical. Its median launch in a decode step fell from 4.5 µs to 1.5 µs (measured), and no end-to-end number moved. The lookup is under 0.1% of a step either way, so the tokens per second stayed where they were. A faster kernel only helps if the step was waiting on it. That is why every chapter measures where the time goes before it changes anything.

entries.title: on an H100 SXM, the ridge moves to 295
entries.text: The roofline carries to any GPU: its ridge is the compute peak divided by the bandwidth. Here that is about 110 FLOP per byte. An H100 SXM is published at 989 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 and 3.35 TB/s, so its ridge sits at about 300, about 2.8 times as far right. Its slope is higher too: Llama 3 8B's about 15 GB of weights read in about 4.5 ms, where TinyLlama needs about 6.4 ms here. Decode does not move. A matrix times one vector does about one FLOP per weight byte on any GPU, because that ratio comes from the model, not the hardware. So batch-1 decode is even further left of the H100's ridge: about 300 rows would have to share each weight read to reach it, against about 110 here. A faster GPU makes the memory wall taller, not lower. These numbers are calculated from published specs, and nothing was measured on an H100 SXM. Its ridge is a ratio of two peaks from a spec sheet, not a measured roofline like this chapter's, whose ceilings came from tests on this GPU; measured ceilings would likely sit below both peaks, as this GPU's bandwidth does below its rated speed.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: Decoding one token reads every weight once, so its floor is bytes ÷ bandwidth: 2.07 GB ÷ 323.6 GB/s, about 6.4 ms, whatever the arithmetic costs. An op's FLOPs per byte decides what limits it. Below the ridge, about 110 FLOP per byte on this GPU, it waits on memory; above it, on compute. Batch-1 decode sits far below. The levers are fewer trips to DRAM: fuse kernels so data stays on chip, and batch requests so each weight byte serves many rows.

entries.title: what GEMM and GEMV mean
entries.text: GEMM is short for general matrix multiply, and GEMV for general matrix-vector multiply. The names come from BLAS, the Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms, a Fortran library first published in 1979 whose routine names every GPU math library still uses: GE for a general matrix, with no special shape such as symmetric or triangular, MM for a matrix times a matrix, MV for a matrix times a vector. Both compute the same thing. Every output value is a dot product: take one row of the left matrix and one column of the right one, multiply them pair by pair and add up the products. An output of M rows and N columns with K pairs in each dot product costs M × N × K multiply-adds. In a transformer the left side is x, the activations, one row for every token being processed, and the right side is a weight matrix W learned in training. Decoding one token makes x a single row, and the product is a GEMV; sending several rows through at once makes it a GEMM. The formula is the same, but the work done for every byte read is not, and that is what the rest of this chapter is about.

entries.title: most of a layer is matrix products
entries.text: Most of a transformer is matrix multiplication. Each of TinyLlama's 22 layers multiplies the hidden state by four weight matrices: QKV (the three attention inputs, stored as one matrix), the attention output, gate/up (the MLP's two widening projections, also one matrix) and down. After the last layer the LM head turns the hidden state into one score for every token of the vocabulary. The engine does not have its own kernel for any of them. All five go through one call to cuBLAS, NVIDIA's library, and this page is about why that is the right call here and how close it gets to the hardware.

entries.title: one row uses each weight byte once
entries.text: Decoding one token means x has one row. A matrix times a vector reads every weight exactly once and uses it for exactly one multiply-add: about one FLOP for every byte. The GPU can do far more arithmetic than that per byte it reads, so the arithmetic is free and the time is the time it takes to read the weights. Every token reads all the weights, which sets a floor of about 6.4 ms per token on this GPU (calculated). cuBLAS sees the single row and runs a dedicated gemv kernel instead of a GEMM.

entries.title: cuBLAS already reads at the roof
entries.text: Dividing the bytes each projection reads by its time in the profile gives its bandwidth. All five reach 99 to 110% of the bandwidth a plain copy kernel measures on this GPU. That test is a measurement, not a physical limit, so a kernel that streams its bytes a little better can pass 100%. A hand-written GEMV could not do better: it has to read the same bytes through the same memory. That is why the engine's own kernels went elsewhere. The projections are about 95% of a decode step's GPU time and already at the roof; the gains were in the launch gaps (CUDA Graphs) and in attention.

entries.title: sixteen rows share one weight read
entries.text: With a batch of requests decoding together, x has a row for each. Each weight row is still read once, but now it meets every one of those input rows, so the FLOPs per byte grow with the batch. That is still far left of the ridge, so the GPU is still waiting on memory, and the projections take about the same time as for one row: about 6.3 ms per step. Sixteen tokens for the price of one is where batching gets its throughput. cuBLAS switches to tensor-core GEMM kernels at this size; the call is the same.

entries.title: a long prompt crosses the ridge
entries.text: A prompt's tokens go through the projections together, so a weight byte meets every row of the prompt. In the largest-batch profile the prefill step is several prompts together, far past the ridge in FLOPs per byte (calculated from config.json). Its projection GEMMs reach about 94% of the compute roof, from their measured time. The GPU now waits on arithmetic, not on bytes. That is why prefill needs the tensor cores, and why prefill and decode want different things from a scheduler: a decode step takes more rows for almost no extra time, a prefill step does not. The chunked prefill chapter is about that. Time to first token shows the same split. At a short prompt the engine's prefill costs 86 µs per prompt token, a small fraction of what a single-request decode step costs per token. It stays almost flat per token as prompts grow, as it does for llama.cpp, whose TTFT works out to a high TFLOP/s rate (calculated). That was not always so: prefill used to run paged decode attention once per row, so the KV reads grew with the square of the length and the cost per token climbed. The FlashAttention prefill chapter replaces that attention with a kernel that runs on the tensor cores too.

entries.title: no decode op gets near the ridge
entries.text: A roofline puts each op at its FLOPs per byte and its speed, under two measured ceilings: the bandwidth on the slope, the compute peak from square cuBLAS GEMMs on the flat part. Switch between the three row counts on the right: the projections slide up the slope, attention moves up only a little, because every row reads its own keys and values, and the prefill projections sit on the flat part. Nothing in a decode step gets near the ridge at about 110 FLOP/byte, so no decode op is compute bound. A long prefill is compute bound, far to its right. The way past the roof in decode is fewer bytes per token: quantized weights, or more rows sharing each weight read.

entries.title: on an H100 SXM, a GEMM needs 295 rows to pass the ridge
entries.text: Carry the projections to Llama 3 8B in BF16 on an H100 SXM. Its hidden state is 4,096 numbers where TinyLlama's is 2,048, and it has 32 layers, so one decode step at one row reads about 15 GB of weights, every weight but the embedding table, where TinyLlama reads about 2.1 GB. Each weight still feeds one multiply-add: two FLOPs for two bytes, one FLOP per byte. Bigger matrices do not change that ratio; only the rows do. With M rows sharing each read, a projection does about M FLOPs per weight byte, so the ridge can be read as a row count. The H100 SXM's ridge is about 300 FLOP per byte, so a projection there turns compute bound at about 300 rows, against about 110 on this GPU. A batch of 16 sits at about 16 FLOP per byte on both, far left of either ridge: on the bigger GPU a decode batch waits on memory even more. These are ideal ratios calculated from published specs. This chapter's measured times come from cuBLAS on this GPU; nothing was run on an H100 SXM or with Llama 3 8B, so where a real kernel turns compute bound there is not measured.

entries.title: a row-major W is a free Wᵀ
entries.text: The model stores W as [out, in] in row-major order, one output row after the other. cuBLAS, which comes from Fortran, reads every matrix column-major. Read column-major with a leading dimension of in, the same bytes are [in, out]: Wᵀ, with no copy. So the wrapper asks for the transposed problem. With the first operand transposed, cuBLAS computes W · Xᵀ, which is Yᵀ, and Yᵀ written column-major is exactly Y in row-major memory. One call, BF16 inputs and output, FP32 accumulation.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: The wrapper asks cuBLAS for the transposed product so row-major weights and activations can stay where they are. No copy or transpose in memory is needed. Below the ridge at about 110 FLOP per byte, memory traffic limits speed. A single decode row uses each weight once, so faster arithmetic does little. Batching lets each weight read serve several token rows. The measured batch still waits on memory, so it produces more tokens in about the same projection time. Prefill is on the other side of the ridge. At 1,024 rows each weight read feeds every row, about 610 FLOP per byte (calculated), and the measured prefill projections reach about 94% of the compute roof. There the tensor cores limit the time, not memory.

entries.title: what the memory has to hold
entries.text: Speed was the subject so far. This chapter is about room. The GPU has about 8.5 GB of memory, and two things must live in it for a token to be decoded: the model's weights, and the KV cache, the keys and values of every token the running requests have seen. The weights are a fixed cost. TinyLlama's are about 2.2 GB, 26% of the memory, and they are the same for one request or a hundred. The cache is the part that grows: every token of every request adds to it, and it is what a longer context or a larger batch has to pay for. The engine settles the split once, at start. It loads the weights, asks the GPU how much memory is free, and takes 90% of that as one pool of cache blocks: about 13,000 blocks, about 4.7 GB. Nothing is allocated later, so a request can never fail on memory halfway through an answer. It can only be made to wait for blocks. The budget is then one line: the tokens in all running requests, times the bytes one token leaves behind, must fit in the pool.

entries.title: a cached token costs 22,528 bytes, whatever it says
entries.text: When a token goes through a layer, attention stores its key and its value so that later tokens can look back at it. That happens in all 22 layers. A key is 4 heads of 64 numbers, a value the same, and a number is 2 bytes. Multiply it out: 22,528 bytes per token. The size does not depend on the token. A comma costs what a rare word costs. So the cache of a request is its length times a constant, and a full context of 2,048 tokens is about 46 MB. The engine hands the memory out in blocks of 16 tokens, 360 KB each; the paged KV cache is about why. One design choice is hidden in the count of heads. TinyLlama has 32 query heads but only 4 key and value heads, which the query heads share in groups. With a key and a value per query head the same token would cost 180,224 bytes, 8 times as much.

entries.title: batch size and context length share one pool
entries.text: The pool holds 206,624 tokens, in every block but block 0, the null block that is never handed out. It does not care whose they are. One request with a long context and many requests with short ones draw on the same blocks, so the two numbers people ask about, how many requests and how long each, are one budget: batch × context ≤ 206,624. For TinyLlama on this GPU the budget is generous. The model itself stops at 2,048 positions, and 100 requests could each reach that before the pool ran out. At the 16 requests the benchmarks run, full contexts would use 16% of the pool. Past 100 the pool becomes the limit: 256 requests can each reach 800 tokens, not 2,048. In practice requests are far shorter than the limit. The batch sweep ran 256 at once and they held at most about 2,000 blocks, 16% of the pool (measured). So here the batch is limited by the time of a step, not by memory. When the pool does fill, the scheduler makes a request wait or takes its blocks back; the next chapter is about those rules.

entries.title: a larger model squeezes the pool from both sides
entries.text: TinyLlama is small, which is why the pool looked endless. Take a model people serve, Llama 3 8B, on the same GPU. In BF16 its weights are about 16 GB: about 8.7 GB more than there is room for. Before any question of batch or context, the weights have to fit. On an H100 SXM with 80 GB they do, with a pool of about 58 GB beside them; the next chapter counts that one. Store each weight in 4 bits and they take about 4 GB. Now there is a pool, but a smaller one, about 3 GB, and each token costs more, 131,072 bytes, because the model has more layers, more KV heads and wider heads. The pool holds about 23,000 tokens: 11 contexts of 2,048 tokens where TinyLlama had 100. Both sides of the budget moved against the batch. Llama 2 7B shows what the head count is worth. Its weights are a little smaller, but every query head has its own key and value, so a token costs 524,288 bytes, 4 times as much, and 3 contexts fit. That is one reason later models share KV heads. Quantization comes back to storing weights in fewer bits.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: The weights take about 2.2 GB of 8.5 GB whatever the load (calculated); the engine gives 90% of what is free after them to one KV pool, about 4.7 GB (measured). A cached token is 22,528 bytes: 22 layers × K and V × 4 KV heads × 64 numbers × 2 bytes (calculated). Batch × context cannot pass 206,624 tokens. 100 requests fit at the full 2,048-token context; 256 can each reach 800 (calculated).

entries.title: the path of one token
entries.text: Ask the engine "What is the capital of Canada?" and it answers "The capital of Canada is Ottawa." This chapter follows one token of that answer, "Ott", from the text of the question to the moment it is an ID, and gives the measured time of every stage on the way. A language model does not write a sentence. It writes one token, a piece of a word, and then it is run again for the next. Each run is called a decode step. The step that produces "Ott" takes in the token before it, "is", and gives back a score for each of the 32,000 tokens the model knows. There are seven stations. Two run on the host, at the ends: text becomes IDs, and an ID becomes text. Five run on the GPU: a lookup, 22 layers, a norm, the LM head and the sampler. The layers take about 70% of a token, which takes about 8.7 ms in all. The rest of the book is about them. Every later chapter opens one station. Read this one for the map.

entries.title: text becomes IDs on the host, once
entries.text: The model has never seen a letter. It knows 32,000 tokens, each with a number, and the tokenizer's job is to cut text into them. First the chat template wraps the question in the markers TinyLlama was trained with. Then SentencePiece cuts the result into 22 pieces and looks up the ID of each. This runs on the CPU and it is cheap: about 17 µs for the whole prompt, measured. It also happens only once per request, before the first step. Against a decoded token of about 8.7 ms it is about 0.2%. The 22 IDs then go through the model together in one step, the prefill, which fills the cache that every later step reads. FlashAttention prefill is about that step. After it the engine decodes: one token in, one token out. Five tokens into the answer the text so far is "The capital of Canada is", and the token going in is "is", ID 338.

entries.title: one ID goes through 22 layers, and that is the token's time
entries.text: On the GPU the ID first becomes a row of 2,048 numbers: the embedding kernel copies row 338 of a table, in 900 ns. That row is the token's stream. Every layer reads it, adds something to it and passes it on. A layer is the same ten operations each time. Attention lets the token look at the tokens before it: a matrix product makes its query, key and value, RoPE marks them with the position, write_kv stores the key and the value, and paged attention scores the query against all 27 keys in the cache. Then an MLP works on the token alone: widen, gate, narrow. Before each half, add + RMSNorm folds the last result into the stream. The last pages of this chapter take attention apart step by step. One layer takes about 270 µs, and 22 of them about 6 ms in 221 kernels. The four matrix products hold 94% of that, and the widest alone, the gate/up projection, 48%. They are slow for one reason: each reads its whole weight matrix from memory for a single token. The GEMM chapter explains it. Attention, the famous part, is about 10 µs per layer.

entries.title: 2,048 numbers become 32,000 scores, then one ID
entries.text: After the last layer the stream is still 2,048 numbers. One more norm rescales it (2.2 µs). Then the LM head multiplies it by a matrix with one row per token of the vocabulary and gives 32,000 scores, the logits. It is one more matrix product: about 370 µs. Here the model has an opinion. After "The capital of Canada is" the largest logit is about 17 for "Ott". The next is about 12 for "Toronto". A gap of 5.1 in logits is a factor of about 160 between the two probabilities, so this step is not a close call. The sampler turns the scores into one choice. This run is greedy: one kernel finds the largest logit and writes its index, 13476, in about 7.1 µs. With a temperature it would draw from the scores instead; the sampling chapter covers how. The host reads the ID back and turns it into text, " Ott", in a few microseconds. The same ID is the input of the next step.

entries.title: the whole trip, timed
entries.text: Put the stages on one line and to one scale. A token takes about 8.7 ms. The 22 layers are about 70% of it and the LM head about 4.2%. The embedding, the final norm and the sampler together are about 0.12%: you cannot see them on the bar. Two parts are not kernels at all. The GPU waits a few microseconds before each kernel it is handed, and with 224 kernels in a step those gaps add up to about 1.2 ms, about 13%. CUDA Graphs removes most of them. And between two steps the host reads the token back, checks for the end and builds the next step: about 1.1 ms, about 13%. So the tokenizer and the sampler, the two ends people picture first, are not where a token's time goes. The time is in reading weights, layer after layer. The next chapter, foundations, says why that read cannot be made much faster, and the last one, where the time went, comes back to this bar after every kernel in the book has changed.

entries.title: on an H100 SXM, Llama 3 8B needs 4.48 ms at least
entries.text: Most of a token is reading weights, so a token has a floor: the bytes a step reads divided by the bandwidth. Here a step reads every weight but the embedding table, of which it copies one row: about 2.1 GB. At about 320 GB/s, the measured bandwidth, that takes about 6.4 ms, and the measured token takes about 8.7 ms: the floor is about 74% of the token. Carry it to a model and a GPU people serve: Llama 3 8B in BF16 on an H100 SXM. Its weights are about 16 GB, about 7.3 times TinyLlama's, and a step reads about 15 GB of them. The H100 reads memory at 3.35 TB/s, about 10 times this laptop GPU, so its floor is about 4.5 ms. A bigger model on a faster GPU, and the token is still set by the same division. These numbers are calculated from published specs; nothing was measured on an H100 SXM or with Llama 3 8B. A real token there would take longer than its floor, as it does here, by an amount this engine never measured.

entries.title: three vectors per token
entries.text: Every token reaches attention as a vector of 2,048 values. One matrix multiply turns it into three vectors: a query, what this token is looking for; a key, what it offers to tokens that look at it; and a value, what it passes on when it is picked. In TinyLlama the query keeps all of those values and the key and the value are only 256 each. That is the QKV projection of the GEMM chapter, and the key and value are what the KV cache stores.

entries.title: score, weigh, sum
entries.text: The newest token compares its query with the key of every token so far: one dot product each, divided by √64 so the scores do not grow with the vector length. A high score means a good match. Softmax turns the scores into weights that are all positive and add up to 1, so the best match gets the largest share: here "cat" gets 42%. The output is the values added up with those weights, one vector per head. That is the whole formula, out = softmax(q · Kᵀ / √d) · V. Chapter 6, paged attention, and the attention chapters after it are about reading K and V fast.

entries.title: only the past
entries.text: A token may only look at itself and the tokens before it; the future is masked out. In prefill every prompt token does this at once, a triangle of scores, 36 of them for the prompt shown. In decode only the newest token is new, so a step adds one row to the triangle: one query against every key so far. Old queries are never used again, but every old key and value is read again at every step. That is why the cache keeps K and V, and not Q.

entries.title: heads, and heads that share
entries.text: Attention runs as 32 heads side by side. The query is cut into one piece per head, each head scores and sums on its own, looking for its own pattern, and the outputs are joined back into one vector. TinyLlama uses grouped-query attention: it has only a few key heads and value heads, and each serves a whole group of query heads. So a token caches 22,528 bytes over all its layers, where one key head per query head would need several times as much. The same memory then holds 8 times the tokens. For the recorded run's pool, the figure shows the two token counts.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: Text becomes IDs once per request on the host: 22 tokens in about 17 µs (measured), about 0.2% of one decoded token. A decode step takes one ID in and gives one ID out. Its 22 layers take about 6 ms of a token (measured; the whole token takes about 8.7 ms), and the four matrix products are about 94% of that. The LM head turns 2,048 numbers into 32,000 logits in about 370 µs, and the greedy sampler keeps one ID in about 7.1 µs (measured). Attention gives each token a query, a key and a value. The newest token's query is scored against every key so far, a softmax turns the scores into weights, and the output is the values summed with them.

entries.title: what paged attention is
entries.text: Attention is the one place in a transformer where tokens look at each other. Each of TinyLlama's 22 layers has one, between a normalization and the MLP, and everything else in a layer works on every token alone. Chapter 1 takes attention apart step by step. In short: each token becomes a query, a key and a value; the newest token's query is scored against every key in the cache, its own included; a softmax turns the scores into weights; and the output is the values summed with those weights. Paged is borrowed from operating systems, where virtual memory cuts a program's memory into fixed-size pages that can sit anywhere and are found through a page table. Paged attention, introduced with vLLM in 2023, does the same with the KV cache: keys and values live in blocks, a block table says where each of a sequence's blocks sits, and the kernel looks every key up there before scoring it. The arithmetic is unchanged; only where each key is read from changes. The next pages follow where those keys and values come from and why they end up in blocks. Then the kernel itself.

entries.title: prefill: the whole prompt at once
entries.text: The prompt is known before generation starts, so the model takes all of it in one pass: every position goes through every layer side by side, and each layer writes the keys and values of every position into the KV cache. Time to first token is this pass. On this engine a long prompt takes about 160 ms, and a prompt token costs about the same in a long prompt as in a short one.

entries.title: decode: one token at a time
entries.text: After the prompt the model emits one token per step, and each token is the input of the next, so steps cannot overlap. A step computes little for one new position, but it reads every weight and every cached key and value. Counted from the model config, with one request in flight the engine reaches 83% of the GPU's measured peak memory bandwidth: the step waits on memory, not on arithmetic.

entries.title: why the cache exists
entries.text: Prefill computes the keys and values of the prompt once and writes them to the KV cache. Decode reads them back. Without the cache every new token would rerun the whole prefill over a context that grew by one. One decode step at a context as long as the prompt took about 18x less time than the prefill that built the cache. Both times are in the caption.

entries.title: the cache has to live somewhere
entries.text: The cache grows by one token per step for every request in flight, and nobody knows in advance how long an answer will be. Reserving the longest possible answer for every request leaves memory the others could use. So the cache is cut into 16-token blocks handed out as a sequence grows, all from one shared pool. Paged attention is the kernel that reads them back, and how it does that is next.

entries.title: one query against every cached key, every step
entries.text: Each decode step adds one token to every sequence. Attention compares that token's query with the key of every token before it, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and sums the values with those weights. 32 query heads against a context that grows by one token every step.

entries.title: every key is found through the block table
entries.text: The KV cache is one pool of 16-token blocks shared by every request. A sequence owns a list of blocks, its block table, and they can sit anywhere in the pool. So the kernel cannot read a context as one contiguous array: every key goes through the table first.

entries.title: pages move the reads, not the math
entries.text: Inside a block, one KV head's 16 keys sit side by side, 64 values each, so a key is one run of 128 bytes and the reads only jump at a block boundary. The table adds one read per key, an integer that the 16 keys of a block share. The scores, the softmax and the weighted sum are the arithmetic of ordinary attention, which is why the tests can check scattered block tables against a CPU reference. What the lookup costs in time was not measured on its own.

entries.title: at 8,192 tokens, Llama 3 8B reads 1.07 GB of K and V a step
entries.text: Carry the read to a model people serve. Llama 3 8B in BF16 caches 131,072 bytes a token, so at its full context of 8,192 tokens one decode step's attention reads 8,192 × 131,072 bytes, about 1.1 GB, for one request, counting each cached byte once. TinyLlama at 2,048 tokens reads about 46 MB. The same step reads the weights too, about 16 GB against TinyLlama's about 2.2 GB. For one request the cache is still the smaller read, about 6.7% of the weights here and about 2.1% for TinyLlama. But the weights are read once a step whatever the batch, and the cache once per request: 16 requests at the full context read about 17 GB of K and V, more than the weights. So once contexts are long and batches full, reading the cache costs as much as reading the weights. These numbers are calculated from published specs; this chapter's kernel was never run on Llama 3 8B's shapes or on an H100 SXM.

entries.title: an online softmax removed v1's context cap
entries.text: The first kernel, v1, kept every score of the context in shared memory and made three passes over it, which capped the context at 2,048 tokens. The second, v2, streams keys in chunks with an online softmax, shares each key between a group of lanes and has no cap; its tests reach 8,192 tokens. Attention per decode step: about 270 µs, down from v1's time in the caption. How the online softmax works is the chapter attention v2.

entries.title: splitting the context filled an idle GPU
entries.text: v2 still launches one block per row and query head, which at one row is a fifth of what the GPU holds at once. Cutting each context into ranges that run side by side, then merging them, took one row at a long context down to about 61 µs. The runner picks a split count every step and runs v2 when it picks one. The chapter split attention has the occupancy measurements, the merge and the CUDA Graphs fix.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: The KV cache is one pool of 16-token blocks, and a block table says where each of a sequence's blocks sits. The kernel looks every key up there, so the arithmetic is unchanged and only where each key is read from changes. An online softmax lets the kernel read keys in chunks. It keeps a running max, a running sum and an accumulator, and when a chunk raises the max it scales the sum and accumulator down instead of rereading earlier chunks. That removes v1's need to hold every score at once, and with it the context cap. When a kernel launches too few blocks to fill the GPU, cutting one long context into ranges and merging the partial results can speed it up: 2.8x here. With enough rows the blocks already exist, so splitting mostly ties or loses.

entries.title: what a paged KV cache is
entries.text: A transformer writes one token at a time, and each new token looks back at every token before it: in each of the 22 layers its query is scored against the key of every earlier token, and the scores mix their values, as chapter 1 showed. The keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so the engine keeps them instead of computing them again on every step. That store is the KV cache, K for keys and V for values. Each new token is computed once, adds one row of keys and one row of values in every layer, and from then on is only read. For TinyLlama a row is the KV heads of one layer in bfloat16, so every token a request sees adds 22,528 bytes over all the layers. Paged means the cache is not one long array per request. Its memory is cut into blocks of 16 tokens, handed out one at a time as a request grows, wherever one is free, and each request keeps a block table that says which block holds each run of its tokens, the first block's worth, the next and so on, the way an operating system finds a program's memory through page tables. That lets many requests share one pool. How the engine decides which of them run together is chapter 17.

entries.title: nobody knows a request's length, so hold only the blocks it fills
entries.text: Every token a request has seen leaves a key and a value in every layer, and attention reads all of them again on every step. When a request arrives nobody knows how long it will get: a chat answer can stop after a few tokens or run to 2,048. A cache with one contiguous row per request has to reserve the worst case up front. The first four requests of a recorded chat run would have reserved far more that way. Taken one block at a time, as they grew, they needed 26 blocks. The idea is the one behind virtual memory: fixed-size pages, handed out on demand, wherever there is room.

entries.title: one pool, a table per request
entries.text: At startup the engine takes a large share of the GPU in one allocation: about 13,000 blocks, each a block of tokens' keys and values for every layer. The first block is never handed out, so a table entry that points at it can mean "nothing here". The block manager keeps, per request, its length and its block table, the list of blocks it owns in order. A position of the first request falls in one of its logical blocks, the table names the physical block behind it, and so it lives in slot 436. The table comes straight from the run: the request's blocks are scattered across the pool between those of the requests running beside it.

entries.title: a new block only every 16 tokens
entries.text: A prefill takes blocks for the whole prompt at once: the first request's 36 prompt tokens fill its first few blocks. After that, every decode step appends one slot per running request. Most of the time the slot is in a block the request already holds; only when its length reaches a multiple of the block size does append_slot take a new one. The new block is the lowest free one. Over its decode steps the request asked for a block 7 times, and the most a request ever leaves empty is the rest of its last block, one slot short of a full block.

entries.title: freed blocks go out again first
entries.text: When a request finishes, every block in its table goes back to the pool, and because the lowest free id goes out first, the next request that needs a block takes those. In the recorded run one of the first request's blocks had already served another request. Every request of the run fit in the first 63 blocks after the null block. That is the block manager of this chapter, and these block ids come from replaying the run by its rules. The run itself had the prefix cache of chapter 19 on, which keeps a finished request's full blocks for later requests and hands out blank blocks first, so the engine's own ids differ. If the pool does run out, the scheduler takes a running request's blocks back and recomputes its tokens later. Which request it picks, what that request loses and why its output does not change is chapter 17.
