entries.title: on Llama 3 8B a cached token is 131,072 bytes
entries.text: Carry the cache to a model people serve: Llama 3 8B in BF16. A cached token costs 2 × 32 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 numbers × 2 bytes, 131,072 bytes, about 5.8 times TinyLlama's 22,528. A block of 16 tokens grows from about 360 KB to about 2.1 MB. Its full context is 8,192 tokens, 4 times TinyLlama's 2,048, so a cache that reserves the worst case holds 512 blocks, about 1.1 GB, for every request however short it stays. The first four requests of the recorded run, at the same lengths in tokens, would hold 2,048 blocks that way, about 4.3 GB. Paged, they hold the same 26 blocks as before, about 55 MB: the reservation grew 4 times, what they use did not. The bound on waste does not change either: a request leaves at most 15 slots of its last block empty, about 2 MB here. These numbers are calculated from published specs; nothing was run with Llama 3 8B.

entries.title: write_kv is a pure copy, one thread per value
entries.text: write_kv is the kernel that fills the slots. After the QKV projection and RoPE, each token's row holds its query heads and then its key heads and value heads. write_kv runs one thread per (token, KV head, dimension), looks up the token's slot, and copies one key and one value bit for bit into the block and the row inside it that the slot names. The cache is laid out by block, then KV head, then token, then dimension, so one head's keys in a block are one contiguous tile, which is what the attention kernel reads. Padding rows get an empty slot and write nothing. It is a pure copy: about 22 µs per single-request decode step over one launch per layer, a small share of the kernel time. The layout and the kernel's tests came before the kernel, and the tests were checked against nine deliberately broken kernels first. Joe's kernel then passed them, and one of them caught two slips in the spec: a QKV row with no query columns was accepted, and an empty batch returned before its arguments were checked.

entries.title: a busy run held 63 of 12,915 blocks
entries.text: On the right is the whole recorded run, replayed through this chapter's allocation rules at half speed: chat requests arriving at a steady rate, up to 8 at once. Each block shows the request that holds it and how full it is. Drag the slider to stop at any step. At its busiest the run held 63 blocks, a tiny part of the pool. The pool is simply most of the memory left after the weights, so a run like this leaves almost all of it free, room for many more or much longer requests. Serving them side by side from one pool is what batching needs: a full batch serves many times the tokens per second of a single request (CUDA Graphs on, both). How the scheduler decides which requests share a step, and how many fit, is chapter 17.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: Nobody knows a request's final length when it arrives, so a contiguous row must reserve the worst case. Handing out 16-token blocks as the request grows took about 6.2% of what worst-case reservation would have taken at the recorded run's busiest step. A request keeps a block table, the list of physical blocks it owns in order, and token pos lives at slot table[pos / 16] · 16 + pos mod 16. The blocks can be anywhere in the pool, so write_kv only has to follow the table. A finished request gives its blocks back and the lowest free id goes out first, so the pool is reused; replayed by these rules, the whole recorded run stays within blocks 1 to 63. If the pool runs out, the newest request is preempted and its tokens are recomputed later, with the same outputs.

entries.title: compute a shared start once
entries.text: Many requests begin with the same tokens. A chat service puts the same system prompt in front of every user message, a second chat turn repeats the whole first turn, and several questions about one document all start with that document. Each of them pays the prefill of those tokens again. It does not have to. A token's keys and values depend only on that token and the ones before it, so the same start gives the same keys and values in every request. Keep them after the first request, and a later request that starts the same way can use them and prefill only the tokens that are its own. That is prefix caching. In this engine, at a shared start of 1,024 tokens and 64 tokens of its own, a request waited 127 ms for its first token without the cache and 24 ms with it (measured).

entries.title: same start, same keys and values
entries.text: In one token, end to end, every layer turns each token into a query, a key and a value, and attention lets a token look only at the tokens before it. So a token's key and value are computed from that token and everything before it, and from nothing after it. Take two prompts that begin with the same words and then differ. Up to the first different token, every key and value is computed from the same inputs, so they are the same numbers. From the first different token on, they differ. The shared start's keys and values do not depend on what follows it. That is what makes them reusable: computed once for the first request, they are exactly what the second request would compute for the same tokens.

entries.title: every block is keyed by its prefix
entries.text: The engine already keeps keys and values in blocks of 16 tokens, the paged KV cache. The cache shares whole blocks, so it needs a way to name a block's contents: a key to look it up by. A block's own 16 tokens are not enough, because its keys and values also depend on every token before it. So the key of a block is every token from the start of the sequence to the end of that block. Two blocks with the same key really do hold the same numbers. The block manager hashes that run of tokens to find the block fast in a map, and keeps the tokens themselves to compare on a hit, since two different runs can share a hash. A match walks the new prompt block by block and stops at the first block it does not find, so it can only ever find a start.

entries.title: two block tables, one physical block
entries.text: A request finds its keys and values through its block table, the list of pool blocks that hold its tokens in order. Nothing stops two tables from listing the same block. So when a new prompt starts with cached blocks, admission puts those same physical blocks into the new request's table and takes fresh blocks only for the rest. Each block keeps a count of the sequences that hold it. A shared block is never written into: a block is shared only once every one of its tokens has its keys and values, and a sequence only ever writes past them. The request's prefill then starts after its cached tokens, in plain, flash and chunked prefill alike, and its rows read the shared keys through its own table. The last prompt token is always computed, even when the whole prompt is cached: its row gives the logits that pick the first new token. So a block that ends at the last token is never matched.

entries.title: published when its step ends
entries.text: A block can be shared only once its keys and values are written. So the scheduler publishes blocks when a step finishes: every full block whose keys and values that step wrote goes into the map, prompt blocks after a prefill and a block of generated tokens when a decode step fills it. Generated tokens count too. A second chat turn sends the first turn and its answer back, followed by a new question, and it finds both the question and the answer in the cache. One case gains nothing: requests admitted in the same step. Their keys and values are being written during that step, so neither can use the other's, and both compute the shared start. A request admitted in any later step finds it.

entries.title: a released block stays cached
entries.text: When a request finishes, its blocks lose a holder. A block nobody holds any more used to go back to the pool blank. Now a published block keeps its keys and values and stays in the map, and it counts as free: the pool can still hand it out. New blocks come from the blank ones first. Only when no blank block is left does the block manager evict a cached block, the one released longest ago. A request releases its blocks from the end of its table backwards, so the end of a chain goes before its start, and what stays cached is a start a later prompt can still match. An evicted block leaves the map and is handed out like a blank one. In the measured runs the pool of 12,915 blocks never ran out of blank blocks, so nothing was evicted there; the tests cover eviction.

entries.title: a hit leaves only its own prefill
entries.text: The measurement: 32 requests, each a shared start of 256, 512, 1,024 tokens plus 64 random tokens of its own, arriving 2 a second, so a request usually finds the engine idle or decoding. With the cache off a later request waits 41.3 ms, 65.0 ms, 127.1 ms for its first token. With the cache on it waits 19.5 ms, 21.7 ms, 24.4 ms (measured). What is left is the prefill of its own 64 tokens, a step of 14 to 18 ms that grows only a little with the start, because those rows attend to every key before them. So a hit saves the prefill of the shared tokens. The first request is the cold case: it finds nothing and prefills everything. One number here is not understood. At 1,024 shared tokens the first request measured 127.9 ms with the cache on and 157.1 ms with it off, although it does the same work in both; the cause was not found.

entries.title: all at once, the batch fills sooner
entries.text: Now all 32 requests arrive at once. A prefill step takes prompts until their tokens reach a budget of 2,048, so the first step admits 6 at 256, 3 at 512, 1 at 1,024 shared tokens, and none of them can share. Every later admission finds the start and counts only its 64 uncached rows against the budget, so more requests join each prefill step. The batch fills sooner and the engine writes 1.6 times, 2.1 times, 3.0 times the tokens per second, at 256, 512, 1,024 shared tokens (781 against 480, 643 against 309, 523 against 175, measured). The hit rates are block arithmetic. One at a time, 31 of the 32 requests find all 1,024 shared tokens: 31 × 1,024 of 32 × 1,088 tokens is 91.2%, the measured rate. All at once at 256, the 6 requests of the first step find nothing, and the rate falls to 65.0%.

entries.title: same keys, nearly the same answers
entries.text: The GPU tests check what a hit reads: the keys and values it takes from the cache are bit-identical, in all 22 layers, to the ones the request writes when it prefills its whole prompt itself. The answers are compared too, greedy, with the cache on and off, over shared system prompts, repeated prompts, concurrent requests, eviction in a small pool, speculation, chunked prefill and a second chat turn. 52 of 58 outputs are identical. The other 6 split at a near tie: the token picked instead was within 3 BF16 ulps of the best logit. The cache is not what changes them. A hit computes the request's own rows as a separate, smaller piece, and the matrix products round a little differently depending on how many rows a step holds. Chunked prefill cuts a prompt the same way, and with the cache off it splits one of the same requests at the same token.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: A block is shared only whole: its key is every token from the start of the sequence to the end of the block, 16 tokens at a time, and the block of the last prompt token is always computed. A finished step publishes the full blocks it wrote, generated tokens included. A released published block stays cached and counts as free; it is evicted only when no blank block is left, least recently released first. At a 1,024-token shared prefix the later requests' time to the first token fell from 127 to 24 ms, and with all 32 requests at once the engine wrote 3.0 times the tokens per second (measured).

entries.title: what quantization is
entries.text: Where the time went ended on a floor: a decoded token reads every weight once, and nothing can make that read faster than the memory delivers it. The kernels shrank the time above the floor. This chapter is about the floor itself, which is set by one thing: how many bytes the weights take. A weight is a number stored in some bits. The engine stores every weight in BF16: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits that pick a power of two, and 7 mantissa bits that say where inside it the number sits. That is 2 bytes. FP8 E4M3 keeps the same three parts in one byte: 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits. The 4-bit files llama.cpp users download, GGUF Q4, spend about half a byte per weight. Quantization is storing the weights in such a narrower format. Fewer bytes per weight means fewer bytes per token, and the floor moves with them. The price is precision: 3 mantissa bits hold 8 steps in each power of two, where BF16 holds 128. The engine does not run quantized yet. FP8 for its weights and its KV cache is in the tree as stubs with specs and tests, for Joe to write. So this chapter is the plan and the arithmetic: every number in it is calculated, and the measurements arrive when the kernels do.

entries.title: the floor moves with the bytes
entries.text: The floor is a division: the bytes a token reads over the bandwidth that delivers them. A token reads 1.03 billion weights, the four matrices of every layer and the LM head (the embedding gives one row). In BF16 that is 2.07 GB, and at the measured 323.6 GB/s the floor is 6.39 ms. Store the same weights in FP8 and a token reads 1.03 GB: the floor falls to 3.20 ms. At 4 bits it is 0.52 GB and 1.60 ms. Nothing in the division is about kernels. Half the bytes per weight is half the floor. That is the floor, not the token. A token today takes more than its floor, and the parts that are not weights, attention reading the cache, the norms, the gaps between kernels, do not shrink with them. So FP8 weights would gain less than half. How much less is not measured: the kernels are stubs.

entries.title: the arithmetic stays free
entries.text: Reading fewer bytes would not help if the GPU then waited on the math. At batch 1 each weight does one multiply and one add, 2 FLOP. Per byte read that is 1 FLOP in BF16, 2 in FP8 and 4 at 4 bits. Foundations put this GPU's ridge, where the math starts to set the time, at 107 FLOP per byte. Every width is far to the left of it. Even at 16 rows, the engine's largest batch, 4-bit weights do 64 FLOP per byte, 60% of the ridge. All the math of a batch-1 token takes 60 µs at the measured peak, against 3.20 ms of reading in FP8. So turning a narrow weight back into a number as it is used costs time only if it adds a trip to memory. A product that reads the byte and converts it as it multiplies, without writing a wider copy anywhere, stays bound by the read. One caution: the ridge uses the tensor cores' measured peak, and the conversion runs on the ordinary cores, whose rate is not measured here.

entries.title: a scale per row fits the weights into eight bits
entries.text: E4M3 holds 8 values in every power of two from 2^-6 up to 256, then 256 to 448 in steps of 32. 448 is the largest: there is no infinity, and anything larger is held at 448. Below 2^-6, seven more values sit 2^-9 apart, and anything under 2^-10 becomes 0. A scale says what the byte means. The stored byte is e4m3(w ÷ s), and the weight read back is the byte's value × s. The plan gives every output row of a weight matrix its own scale, s = the row's largest |w| ÷ 448, so the largest weight of each row lands exactly on 448 and none saturates. It costs one FP32 number per row: 426,240 for TinyLlama, 0.16% of the FP8 weights' bytes. Dividing by s slides a whole row along the ladder at once. A weight more than 28,672 times smaller than its row's largest lands among the coarse values at the bottom, and one about 458,752 times smaller becomes 0. How many of TinyLlama's weights land there is not measured here.

entries.title: rounding costs at most half a step
entries.text: Between 1 and 2, E4M3 has 8 values: 1, 1.125, 1.25 and so on to 1.875. A weight between two of them rounds to the nearer one, so it moves by at most half a step, 0.0625: 1/16 of the power of two it sits in. Every power of two has the same 8 steps, so the bound holds across the normal range. BF16 has 128 steps in the same place, so it moves a weight by at most 1/256. Going from BF16 to FP8 makes each weight's possible error 16 times larger. The rounding happens once, when the weights are written, and costs nothing per token. What it does to the model's answers is another question, and this chapter cannot answer it. Small errors in many weights partly cancel and partly add up through 22 layers. The spec leaves it to the wiring: the logit error against the reference, before and after. Until then the effect on TinyLlama's output is not measured.

entries.title: an FP8 cache holds twice the tokens
entries.text: The weights are not the only bytes. The memory budget counted 22,528 bytes for each cached token in BF16. The cache can be stored as E4M3 the same way, and then a token costs 11,264 bytes. The pool keeps its size, 4.66 GB, so it holds twice the blocks: 413,264 tokens where it held 206,624, 201 full contexts of 2,048 tokens where 100 fit. For TinyLlama memory was not the limit, so on this GPU that is room nobody needs yet. For a larger model whose pool is small, it is a longer context or a larger batch. The spec is plain that it will not make attention faster yet: attention is far from its bandwidth roof at batch 16, so this is about room first. It uses one scale for all keys and one for all values, and the wiring starts from a scale of 1, which reaches 448, far above what TinyLlama's keys and values reach.

entries.title: the plan: a dtype and three kernels
entries.text: Three commits put the plan in the tree, for Joe to implement. DType::F8E4M3 is one byte per element, named F8_E4M3 as safetensors spells it, and it is the one piece that is done. The rest are stubs that throw, each with a spec and tests written first. gemm_fp8 is the weight product: y = row_scale × Σ x · w, with x in BF16, w in FP8 and one scale per output row, the sum in FP32 and the result rounded to BF16 once. write_kv_fp8 rounds each step's new keys and values into an FP8 cache, to the nearest value and held at ±448. paged_attention_decode_fp8 reads them back as byte × scale, exact in FP32, and is decode attention from there, held to the tolerance of the other paged kernels. Each rejects a BF16 tensor where FP8 is due. None of it is wired. A later branch writes each row's scale once at load, gives the cache a dtype, puts the FP8 path behind a flag and measures bytes per step, step time and logit error. Real engines already do this: llama.cpp's GGUF files store weights at 2 to 8 bits in small blocks, each block with its own scale, and vLLM serves FP8 weights, an FP8 KV cache, and 4-bit AWQ and GPTQ checkpoints.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: A token reads 2.07 GB of BF16 weights, a floor of 6.39 ms; in FP8 1.03 GB and 3.20 ms; at 4 bits 1.60 ms (calculated). The parts that are not weights do not shrink. E4M3 is 1 sign, 4 exponent and 3 mantissa bits, largest value 448. One scale per row, the row's largest |w| ÷ 448, fits each row into it, and rounding moves a weight by at most 1/16 of its power of two, against 1/256 in BF16. An FP8 cache halves a token's 22,528 bytes, so the same pool holds 413,264 tokens instead of 206,624 (calculated).

entries.title: what RoPE does
entries.text: RoPE is short for rotary position embedding. It is how TinyLlama, like the other Llama models, tells attention where each token sits in the prompt. It was introduced in 2021 in the RoFormer paper. The original transformer added a fixed position vector to each token's embedding once, before the first layer; RoPE works inside every attention layer instead. As chapter 1 showed, attention scores two tokens with the dot product of one's query and the other's key. A dot product only sees the numbers, so without help a query would give a key the same score whether that key's token came just before it or a thousand tokens back. Take two values of a vector as a point on a plane. Turning the point around the centre keeps its length and changes only its direction. RoPE turns each query and each key by an angle proportional to its token's position, so a query and a key three positions apart end up the same angle apart wherever they sit, as the figure shows for two such pairs of positions. The score then changes with the distance between the two tokens and stays the same when both move along together. The figure turns one pair of values. A head has 32 such pairs, each turning at its own rate.

entries.title: a turn by position encodes the gap
entries.text: Attention compares every query with every key, and on its own it has no idea which token came first. RoPE gives it the order by turning the query and key vectors, not by adding anything to them. Each head's values are read as 32 pairs, and pair i is turned by the angle position · θᵢ. A query at position p and a key at position p′ then meet at an angle that depends only on p − p′. The first pairs turn fast and tell nearby tokens apart; the last ones barely move and carry the long distances.

entries.title: only Q and K turn, i with i + 32
entries.text: The QKV projection leaves one row of values per token: the query heads, then the key heads, then the value heads. RoPE turns the Q and K heads in place, right before the keys are written to the cache, and leaves V alone. Inside a head, value i pairs with value i + 32, not with its neighbour; that is how Hugging Face's rotate_half lays it out, and the weights were trained that way. Each pair costs one cosine, one sine, four products and two sums.

entries.title: pairs are independent, heads share a sine
entries.text: No pair needs anything from another pair, and at one position every head turns pair i by the same angle. So the fast kernel gives one thread to each pair of a head group, with a few groups, 256 threads per token. Each thread computes the cosine and sine of its pair once and applies them to every head of its group, so no head waits for another. That is far fewer sines and cosines per token than one for every head and pair, and 6.5 µs for one token. Neighbouring threads read neighbouring pairs, so a warp's narrow loads already coalesce into a few contiguous sectors; the wide vector loads of the spec were never needed.

entries.title: position multiplies a last-bit error
entries.text: The naive kernel copies PyTorch's arithmetic exactly: cos and sin in FP32, rounded to BF16, then each product rounded on its own. The fast kernel has to match the naive one bit for bit. The frequencies are the trap. A device powf differs from the host's in the last bit for a couple of the frequencies, the angle multiplies that error by the position, and near 2,047 a sine lands on the other side of a BF16 rounding boundary. The subtraction then turns one ulp into dozens. Both kernels now take the frequencies from a table the host computes.

entries.title: one thread per head leaves most idle
entries.text: Joe's first draft gave each head one thread, so most of a token's threads had nothing to do and each busy one walked its pairs one after another, computing every sine and cosine again for every head. Correct once the frequencies came from the host, but flat at about 22 µs at every token count, slower than the naive kernel at one token. The time was the chain of pairs each thread walked, not the memory: only at the largest token count did the naive kernel get slower.

entries.title: at small counts the launch sets the time
entries.text: For small token counts the fast kernel stays near its one-token time: a few hundred KB at most, far from the memory limit, so the launch and one chain of load, sine and store set the time. At the largest count it is about 18 µs, half the naive kernel's. Try the token counts on the right. In a decode step RoPE is under 1% of the time, so the gain is small in absolute terms. The point was to stop being slower than the kernel it replaced, and to stay bit-identical while doing it.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: RoPE turns query and key pairs by position. For fixed query and key vectors, their attention score depends on the gap between positions and stays the same when both move together. Independent pairs can run in parallel, and heads can share the same sine and cosine. This removes the draft's long chain of pair rotations and avoids repeating trigonometry for every head. Matching the rotation formula is not enough to match the model's bits. The source of the frequencies and the rounding of each product matter, especially at large positions.

entries.title: what sampling is
entries.text: The last layer of the model, the LM head, turns the token's final vector into 32,000 logits, one score for every token in the vocabulary. A logit can be any number, and only the gaps between them matter. Sampling turns those scores into the one token id the model writes next. Softmax makes them probabilities: divide each logit by a temperature T, raise e to it, and divide by the sum over the whole vocabulary. Greedy decoding takes the largest logit, so a prompt always gets the same answer. Sampling draws one token at random with those probabilities. After “The capital of Canada is” TinyLlama puts nearly all its weight on Ott, the start of Ottawa, so both give the same word. After “Once upon a time, a robot named” the likeliest name, Max, gets 9% at the model's own odds: greedy writes Max every time, sampling a different name most times. Temperature sets how bold the draw is. At half the temperature the gaps double and Max rises to 29%; at a higher temperature it falls. Toward zero sampling becomes greedy, and the engine treats a temperature of zero as greedy. The rest of the chapter is how the GPU picks without sorting the vocabulary.

entries.title: greedy is an argmax over 32,000 logits
entries.text: After the LM head, each sequence has 32,000 logits and needs one token id. Greedy decoding takes the largest: a block of threads strides across the row, each keeping the best value and index it saw, and a tree halves them to one. Ties go to the lowest index, so the result never depends on thread timing: about 21 µs per call.

entries.title: sampling is an argmax too
entries.text: Sampling from softmax(logits / T) usually means exponentials, a sum, a running total and a search. The Gumbel-max trick skips all of that: add independent Gumbel noise, −log(−log u), to every scaled logit and take the argmax. The winner is distributed exactly as the softmax. So temperature sampling is the greedy kernel with noise added. The figure draws repeated samples; the picks settle onto the softmax outline.

entries.title: counter-based noise replays exactly
entries.text: The noise comes from Philox, a counter-based generator: token i at decode step s gets the number at offset s × 32,000 + i of the request's seed. Nothing is stored between calls. The same seed repeats a whole answer, and a row draws the same token whether it runs alone or in a batch of 16, which the tests check. Each row carries its own seed, step and temperature, so greedy and sampled requests share one launch.

entries.title: top-k: search for the cut, no sort
entries.text: Top-k keeps the k largest logits. Sorting 32,000 values per row to find them is the usual way. Here the kernel binary-searches a threshold instead: each pass every thread counts its logits at or above the cut, one block sum, and the cut moves up or down. Logits become keys that sort like the floats, and each pass settles one bit of the key, so 32 passes find the exact cut, and every token tied with the k-th largest stays in.

entries.title: top-p: the same search, on mass
entries.text: Top-p keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose probability reaches p. The same search works on mass instead of a count: each pass adds exp(s − max) over the logits at or above the cut and compares it with p times the total. The search starts from top-k's cut when both are set, as in Hugging Face, which applies top-k first.

entries.title: top-k runs 2.1x faster than a bare sort
entries.text: Top-k takes about 130 µs. Sorting the row alone, before any prefix sum or draw, takes about twice as long, so the search wins comfortably. Two columns break the pattern: top-p alone, and plain temperature sampling at about 430 µs, the slowest mode of all.

entries.title: FP64 logs make temperature slowest
entries.text: The noise uses double-precision log. A laptop GPU runs FP64 at a small fraction of its FP32 rate, and Nsight Compute shows the FP64 pipe busy 84% of the time for a small share of the instructions. With temperature alone every token gets noise; with top-k only the kept ones do. A throwaway float version ran in 65 to about 96 µs. It changes which token a fixed seed draws, so it is written up for a decision rather than merged.

entries.title: rows run side by side, one block each
entries.text: Every mode launches one block per row, so a single row uses one of the 26 SMs and each extra row uses another. That is why the times barely change with the batch: the rows run side by side. Try both row counts on the right.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: Adding independent Gumbel noise to the scaled logits and taking the argmax draws from the softmax distribution. The sampler does not need to build that distribution explicitly. Top-k searches for a cut by counting tokens, while top-p searches by adding probability mass. When both are set, top-k goes first, and ties at the cut stay in. A threshold search can cost less than ordering the whole vocabulary. In this benchmark, top-k sampling is 2.1x faster than sorting the row alone.

entries.title: what a scheduler decides
entries.text: A GPU that answered one request at a time would read all of its weights for a single row of work. So the engine runs many requests in the same forward pass: one step, one row for each request that is decoding. Something has to choose, before every step, whose rows those are. That is the scheduler. A request is in one of three states: waiting in a queue, running with KV blocks of its own, or finished. Before each step the scheduler looks at the queue and at the running list and builds the step. The model runs it, one new token comes back for each row, and the scheduler looks again. It makes three decisions. Admission: may the request at the front of the queue start now? Growth: each running request needs room for one more token, so is there a block for it? Preemption: if there is not, who gives memory back? Two things can run out. Memory, because every cached token takes bytes from a pool that is fixed at startup. And time, because every row makes the step longer and every running request waits for the whole step. This chapter is about which of the two runs out first, and what the scheduler does when it happens.

entries.title: every token costs 22,528 bytes of cache
entries.text: The KV cache keeps a key and a value for every token a request has seen, in every layer (chapter 5). For TinyLlama that is 2 × 22 layers × 256 numbers × 2 bytes, 22,528 bytes a token. The cache is handed out in blocks of 16 tokens, about 360 KB each. At startup the engine takes 90% of the memory left after the weights as one pool: about 13,000 blocks on this GPU, about 4.7 GB, room for about 210,000 tokens once block 0 is kept back as the null block. That is the budget. Nothing adds to it while the server runs. A request of length L holds ceil(L / 16) blocks: enough for its prompt when it starts, then one more each time its length reaches a multiple of 16. So a request has no fixed price. It starts small, grows by a block every 16 decode steps, and gives everything back when it finishes.

entries.title: divide the pool by what requests hold
entries.text: How many requests fit is the pool divided by what one request holds, and the question is what to count. Nobody knows on arrival how long a request will get. Its context can run to 2,048 tokens, 128 blocks. Reserve that for each and 100 requests fit, whatever they go on to do. The engine counts what is there: a request holds only the blocks its tokens fill. The requests of a recorded chat run ended at 31 to about 230 tokens. 100 of them hold about 940 blocks, about 7.3% of the pool, and the pool has room for about 1,400 such requests. Drag the slider on the right. The price is that the answer is not known in advance. Requests keep growing after they were let in, so a pool that had room for everyone at admission can still run out later. Preemption, further on, is what the engine does then.

entries.title: the row limit filled first, never the pool
entries.text: There is a second limit, max_batch: the most requests the scheduler runs at once, 16 by default. It is there because of time, not memory. Every running request adds a row to every step, and a step with more rows takes longer: about 9.5 ms at 16 rows, about 64 at 256, measured. Each running request waits one whole step for each of its tokens, so more rows mean more tokens per second in total and a slower answer for everyone. 16 requests that all reach the full 2,048 tokens hold 2,048 blocks, about 16% of the pool, so with max_batch 16 the pool cannot run out. The load runs later in this chapter recorded 0 preemptions over all 4 engine configurations and 7 rates. A request that waited there waited for a row, never for memory. Raise max_batch and memory comes back into play: from 128 on, the worst case is more than the pool. The run at max_batch 256 peaked at only about 2,000 blocks because its requests were short. A larger model shifts the balance the other way: each token costs more bytes and the weights leave less room for the pool.

entries.title: first come, first served, nothing skips ahead
entries.text: Before every step, Scheduler::schedule() looks at the front of the waiting queue. While fewer than max_batch requests are running, it asks the block manager one question: are ceil(L / 16) blocks free, with L the request's whole length so far? If so the request takes those blocks and joins the back of the running list. If not, or if its prompt would push the prompts admitted in this step past max_prefill_tokens, admission stops for this step. Two things follow. The queue is strict: a short request behind a long one waits even when it would fit, so a long request is never starved by a stream of short ones. And only what exists is reserved: blocks for the prompt, none for the answer. The answer's blocks are asked for one at a time, as it grows. A step that admits anyone is the prefill of the requests it admitted, and only of them. Each of them gets its first token from it, and the requests that were already running sit that step out. Chapter 18 is about that wait.

entries.title: a full pool evicts the newest request
entries.text: In a decode step every running request appends one slot. Most of the time it lands in a block the request already holds. When its length is a multiple of 16 it needs a new block, and if none is free the scheduler makes room: the request at the back of the running list, the one admitted last, is the victim. The victim loses every block, so its whole cache is gone. It keeps its prompt and the tokens it has generated, and goes to the front of the waiting queue, ahead of requests that never ran. One eviction frees at least one block, which is all a growing request needs; another request later in the same step can cause another. A request that is itself at the back of the list evicts itself. Once blocks for its whole length are free it is admitted like any other request, and its prefill recomputes the keys and values of the prompt plus the generated tokens, starting at position 0. Nothing the client received is taken back. The same tokens through the same weights rebuild the same cache, so a greedy request continues as if nothing had happened: a test squeezes 16 requests into 56 blocks and compares every output with a roomy run. With sampling it asks for 14 of the 16, since the recomputed values come from a pass of another shape and can differ in their last bits. Evicting from the back means the oldest request is never the victim while a newer one runs, and the scheduler refuses a pool smaller than one full context. So the oldest request can always finish, and the queue always drains.

entries.title: a static batch waits for its longest request
entries.text: Why decide again before every step? The alternative is a static batch: take the first 4 requests, run them together, and take the next group only when every one of them is done. A request that stops early keeps its slot until the longest request in its batch finishes. Here one request runs far longer than the rest of its batch, which is done early. The dashed cells are slots that go through every forward pass and produce nothing: the requests waste 36 slot-steps.

entries.title: continuous batching refills a slot every step
entries.text: Continuous batching, also called iteration-level scheduling, runs the scheduler before every step instead of before every batch. A finished request leaves at once, and the request at the front of the queue takes its slot on the next step. Same queue, room for every request: the requests waste only 8 slot-steps, all of them at the end, when the queue is empty and the last requests drain.

entries.title: a tight pool costs recomputed steps
entries.text: Now give the same queue a pool that is too small: a few blocks, each a couple of steps long where the engine's hold 16 tokens. Admission and preemption both show in the grid. 3 preemptions follow: the crossed cells are evictions and the shaded cells are steps recomputed after one. Every shaded cell is work done twice, which is what preemption costs. The run still wastes 12 slot-steps against the 36 of static batching. The first workbench at the end of this chapter runs the same two rules on a real block pool.

entries.title: on an H100 SXM, Llama 3 8B fits 53 full contexts, not 100
entries.text: Carry the count to a model and a GPU people serve: Llama 3 8B in BF16 on an H100 SXM with 80 GB. The weights take about 16 GB, and the engine's rule, 90% of what is left, gives a pool of about 58 GB. A cached token costs 2 × 32 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 numbers × 2 bytes, 131,072 bytes, about 5.8 times TinyLlama's: more layers, more KV heads, wider heads. So the pool is about 27,000 blocks, room for about 440,000 tokens. A full context is longer too, 8,192 tokens where TinyLlama stops at 2,048: 512 blocks, about 1.1 GB for one request. Divide, and 53 full contexts fit where TinyLlama's pool held 100. The pool grew about 12 times, but what one long request holds grew about 23 times. The rules do not change. With max_batch 16, 16 full contexts hold 8,192 blocks, about 30% of this pool, so the row limit still fills first; with more than 53 long requests running, the pool runs out and preemption is back. These numbers are calculated from published specs, and nothing was measured on an H100 SXM or with Llama 3 8B. A real pool would be a little smaller, since the CUDA context and the engine's own buffers take memory too.

entries.title: goodput peaks at an offered 5 requests a second
entries.text: The test: 120 requests arrive at random times, a Poisson process at 1 to 8 per second, with prompts of 16 to 512 tokens and answers of 16 to 256, and at most 16 run together. Goodput counts the requests per second that got their first token within 500 ms and each later token within 50 ms. Up to 3 per second every request meets both. With whole-prompt steps the engine's best is about 4.5 at an offered 5, and at 8 only 25% of the requests are in time. Its 99th percentile wait for the first token is about 4.6 s at 8 per second, while the median time per token is about 15 ms. The first token misses its limit and the later ones do not: a running request is fine, and the late ones are in the queue, waiting for one of the 16 rows. What running together buys is the other number: offline, a batch of 16 gives about 1,700 tokens per second against about 140 one request at a time. These load runs are from 2026-11-11, with the FlashAttention prefill kernel of chapter 9.

entries.title: vLLM won on kernel speed, not scheduling
entries.text: vLLM served the same token ids at the same arrival times, with the same weights and the same limit of 16 requests. Its goodput reaches about 7.5 at an offered 8, 1.6x the engine's best of about 4.5. The scheduler is not the difference. Both batch continuously and both stop at 16 rows, and neither ran short of memory: no run of either preempted a request. vLLM mixes pieces of prefill into its decode steps; the engine does the same with a token budget (chapter 18) and its best goodput moves from 4.45 to 4.54. The difference is how long the work takes. At 1 per second the engine's median time per token is 9.5 ms and vLLM's 8.8; at 8 it is about 15 against 9.2. In the engine's run at 8 per second, prefill took 3.4 of about 20 seconds, and a decode step averaged about 12 ms, against vLLM's whole time per token of 9.2 ms with its prefill included. These runs already use the FlashAttention prefill kernel of chapter 9, so prefill is the smaller part of the run: the rest of the gap is the decode step at a batch of 16. The comparison even favours the engine: vLLM's times include its HTTP server and a Python client, and the engine's are taken inside the process. Its limits: uniform lengths and random tokens, 120 requests a run, and a cap of 16 that is not vLLM's default.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: Every cached token costs 22,528 bytes, a block is 16 tokens and the pool is about 13,000 blocks. A request holds ceil(length / 16) of them, so 100 requests fit if each reserves the full 2,048 tokens and far more if each holds only what it has written. Admission is first come, first served: the front of the queue starts when a row is free and blocks for its whole length are free, and nothing skips ahead. When a running request needs a block and none is free, the newest running request loses its cache, goes to the front of the queue and is recomputed from position 0. With max_batch 16 the worst case is 2,048 blocks, so the pool cannot fill, and the load runs recorded 0 preemptions. The engine's best goodput was about 4.5 requests per second against vLLM's about 7.5, with the same batching and the same cap.

entries.title: guess ahead, then check
entries.text: So far a decode step has meant one token. The model reads all of its weights, writes one token, and reads them all again for the next. This chapter is about getting several tokens out of one reading. The idea has two halves. First, guess the next few tokens cheaply, without the model. Second, run the model once on the real input and on all the guesses together. Where the model's own choice agrees with a guess, that token is done, and the weights were read once for all of them. Nothing is approximated. A guess is only kept when the model, given the right tokens before it, picks the same token. A wrong guess costs some wasted arithmetic and is thrown away. So the answer is the one plain decoding writes, in fewer steps. In the answer recorded for this chapter, 76 tokens took 26 steps where plain decoding takes 76. The model agreed with 50 of the 117 guessed tokens (measured).

entries.title: a step has rows to spare
entries.text: A decode step for one request reads every weight to produce one token. The first chapters showed that the reading is the cost: the arithmetic for one row is tiny beside it. So a second row in the same step is nearly free, because the weights are read once for all the rows. The numbers say how nearly. One request alone takes about 6.9 ms per token. Sixteen requests in one step take about 8.2 ms: 16 rows for about 1.2 times the price of one (measured). When fewer than 16 requests are running, the other rows go unused. Speculative decoding fills those rows with more tokens of the same request. The trouble is that the tokens after the next one are not known yet. So it guesses them.

entries.title: the guess is copied from the context
entries.text: Many answers repeat their prompt. A summary quotes the text, an edited function is mostly the old function, a list is copied with one change. When the answer is in the middle of such a copy, the next tokens are already on the page, a little earlier. So the engine looks back. It takes the last 3 tokens of the context and searches for the latest earlier place where the same 3 appeared. The tokens that followed them there are the guess, the draft. If there is no match for 3 tokens it tries 2, then 1, and with no match at all there is no draft and the step is a plain one. This is called prompt lookup. In the recorded answer, step 12 found its last token 85 tokens back and copied the next 8 as its guess, “, in every layer. A decode step” in the prompt, and the model agreed with all of them. The search is a scan of the context on the CPU. It needs no second model and no extra pass on the GPU.

entries.title: one step checks every guess
entries.text: The step then runs the real input and the draft together, as rows of the same sequence. Row 0 is the last real token. Row 1 is the first guessed token, row 2 the second, and so on. Each row attends to everything before it, the earlier rows of this step included, the way the rows of a prompt do in prefill. Every row samples a token. Row 0's token is what plain decoding would have produced, so it is always kept. If it equals the first guess, then row 1 was computed from the right input, and its token is kept too. The chain stops at the first row whose guess was wrong: that row's own token is still right, and everything after it was computed from a wrong token and is dropped. So every kept token is the token plain decoding would have sampled. This holds with a temperature too, because the sampler's random number depends on the seed and on the token's place in the answer, not on the step it ran in. In step 1 the model agreed with 2 of 8 guesses, and the step wrote 3 tokens. One caveat is the one batching already has. A step with more rows rounds its BF16 arithmetic a little differently, so where the two best tokens are one rounding step apart, the choice can go the other way. It happened in 4 of the 10 measured prompts, each time at such a near tie.

entries.title: a wrong guess gives its cache slots back
entries.text: Every row writes its key and value into the paged KV cache before attention reads them. That is what lets a guessed row see the guessed rows before it. It also means a rejected row has left a key and a value behind, computed from a token that is not in the answer. The scheduler reserves one slot per row before the step and gives the unused ones back after it. The sequence's length in the block table is cut to the last kept row, and a block that is no longer needed returns to the free list. The next step writes its own key and value over the stale slot before anything reads it. Two rules keep guesses from hurting other requests. A draft only takes rows that no request needs: with 16 requests running there are none, and nothing changes. And a draft never takes a block that would make another request wait: if the pool is short, the draft is shortened instead.

entries.title: it pays when the answer repeats the prompt
entries.text: On four prompts whose answers repeat them (repeat a paragraph, fix its spelling, add a docstring to a function, rename a variable in it), with up to 8 guesses per step, the model agreed with about 22% of the guessed tokens. A step wrote about 2 tokens on average, and the time per token fell from 7.9 to 4.12 ms per token (measured, one request at a time). That is about 1.9 times the tokens per second. Ordinary chat answers have less to copy: there the model agreed with 10% of the guesses. The time per token still fell, from about 7.7 to about 6 ms. A wrong guess only costs a row, and a row is cheap; and chat answers repeat themselves more than one would think. More guesses are not always better: with up to 15 the time per token was 4.14 ms, because the extra rows cost more than the few extra tokens they bring. The spare rows shrink as requests share the step. With 16 chat requests decoding at once, up to 8 guesses each ran at 0.94 times the tokens per second of plain decoding: slower. A limit that halves after a wrong guess and doubles back after a right one ran at 1.01 times. With requests arriving at 4 per second that limit took the median time per token from 8.9 to 7.3 ms, and sampling at temperature 0.7 kept the gain on chat (about 1.3 times, all measured). A small draft model can guess where there is nothing to copy. The engine can run one, and with the one tried it lost: 0.79 times the tokens per second with 2 guesses per step (measured). Beyond this engine says why.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: 16 rows cost about 1.2 times one row: about 8.2 ms against about 6.9 ms per step (measured). A wrong guess wastes a row, not a step. The guess is the tokens that followed the last 3 tokens the last time they appeared in the context. No draft model, no extra pass on the GPU. On answers that repeat their prompt the model agreed with about 22% of the guesses and the time per token fell from 7.9 to about 4.1 ms; on chat answers it agreed with 10% and the time went from about 7.7 to about 6 ms (measured).

entries.title: what splitting attention means
entries.text: While a token is decoded, attention takes that token's query in one head, scores it against every key in the KV cache, turns the scores into weights with a softmax and adds up the cached values with those weights. TinyLlama does this in 32 query heads, and each head's work is one walk along its whole context. The walking is done by the GPU's streaming multiprocessors, or SMs. An SM is one of the GPU's processors, with its own registers, its own fast shared memory and room for several groups of threads at a time; this GPU has 26. A kernel hands its work to the SMs as thread blocks: a block is a group of threads that starts on one SM, stays there until it is done and shares that SM's memory. At batch 1 the attention kernel gets one block per query head, 32 in all, and each walks its head's context alone. That leaves most of the room on the SMs empty, and a longer context only makes every block take longer. Splitting cuts each context into pieces and gives every piece its own block, so more blocks run side by side. A block that has seen only a piece cannot write the answer, so it writes a partial result: the largest score it saw, its sum of exponentials and its weighted values. A second, small kernel combines the pieces into the same answer one walk over the whole context gives.

entries.title: one block per head leaves most of the GPU idle
entries.text: The kernel of the chapter attention v2 launches one thread block per row and query head. At batch 1 that is 32 blocks. Each SM of this GPU holds only a few of them at once (registers and warps both stop it there), so the SMs together have a fixed number of slots. That fills only 0.21 of a wave. Every block walks its head's whole context alone, and most of the GPU has nothing to do.

entries.title: cut each context into ranges, one block each
entries.text: The split kernel adds a grid dimension: blocks are (split, head, row). Each split takes a range of whole KV blocks, so no 16-token block is shared by two ranges, and runs the same online-softmax loop as v2 over it. One head's long context becomes 8 ranges, worked on at the same time.

entries.title: each split writes a partial m, l and sum
entries.text: A split cannot write the output, because it only saw part of the context. It writes three things to a float scratch buffer: its largest score m, its sum of exponentials l, and its 64 weighted values, not yet divided. The buffer was a new argument to the kernel, which is why split attention needed its own signature. The runner owns 67,584 bytes of it.

entries.title: rescaled to one maximum, the merge is exact
entries.text: A second, small kernel, one block per row and head, finds the largest partial maximum, rescales every partial result to it and adds them up in split order. Splits finish in whatever order the GPU runs them, but the merge always adds them the same way, so the same input gives the same bits on every run. One row at a long context now takes about 61 µs per call, merge included. Rescaling to the largest maximum is the step an online softmax takes when a chunk raises its maximum, so the merged result is the same softmax as one pass over the whole context. Only the order of the float additions differs.

entries.title: a CUDA graph replays the split count it captured
entries.text: Wired into the decode step, splitting made a long prompt faster per token in eager mode. With CUDA Graphs nothing moved: each graph had been captured on a dummy batch with no context, where the rule says one split, so every replay launched v2's grid. The fix captures one graph per batch size and split count, more graphs than before, and replays the one that matches the batch: about 9.1 ms.

entries.title: short of warps to switch to, not of bandwidth
entries.text: For v2 at one row, a long context sounds like a lot of memory to read, but Nsight Compute shows DRAM at 1.6% of its peak. The kernel is not short of bandwidth. It is short of warps. A load that has to go to DRAM waits several hundred cycles on this GPU, much longer than one that hits L2, and a GPU hides that wait by running other warps in the meantime. With about 21% of warp slots filled, there are too few to switch to.

entries.title: splits pay until the grid passes one wave
entries.text: Each doubling of the split count doubles the grid. While the whole grid fits in one wave, the time halves each time. At the last doubling the grid is about 1.6 waves. The first wave's worth of blocks run together and the rest wait for a second, mostly empty wave, so each block has half the work and the time barely moves.

entries.title: many rows or a short context: splitting loses
entries.text: With many rows v2 already launches 512 blocks, enough to fill the GPU several times over, and splitting only adds the partial writes and the merge. At a very short context a split holds too few keys to pay for its second launch. So the rule doubles the split count only while the grid stays at or under 256 blocks and each split keeps enough tokens to pay for itself. Try the measured times on the right.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: At batch 1 attention launches one block per query head, 32 blocks, which fills only a fifth of what this GPU can hold. DRAM sits nearly idle, so the kernel is limited by too few warps to hide load latency, not by bandwidth. Cutting each context into ranges multiplies the blocks, and the time roughly halves with every doubling while the grid still fits in one wave. Past that the extra blocks wait for a second, mostly empty wave, and with enough rows the grid is already full, so splitting only adds work. A block that sees only part of the context cannot write the output, so it writes a partial result, and a small merge kernel adds the pieces in split order. That fixed order is why the same input gives the same bits on every run.

entries.title: what SwiGLU is
entries.text: SwiGLU stands for Swish-gated linear unit. A gated linear unit, or GLU, makes two linear projections of the same input and multiplies them value by value: one of them, the gate, decides how much of the other gets through. The first GLU squashed its gate with a sigmoid, which runs from zero to one. SwiGLU, one of the variants Noam Shazeer compared in 2020, puts the gate through Swish instead, which with its parameter at one is the function PyTorch calls SiLU: silu(g) = g × sigmoid(g). In TinyLlama it is the middle of every layer's MLP, the block after attention. The normalized hidden state is projected twice, by a gate matrix and an up matrix, into 5,632 values each. SwiGLU turns each gate and up pair into one value, and the down matrix takes the results back to the hidden size, and they are added onto the hidden state. sigmoid(g) is the share of the gate that silu keeps: about a half at zero, almost none for a strongly negative gate, nearly all of it for a strongly positive one. So a negative gate shuts its up value off and a large one lets it through, scaled by about g. The curve bends smoothly, with a small dip below zero, where a ReLU would cut off at zero with a corner. The gate costs a third matrix. The width is two thirds of the usual four times the hidden size, rounded up to a multiple of a GPU-friendly block size, so the three matrices hold about as many weights as a plain MLP's two that widen to four times the hidden size.

entries.title: each output is silu(gate) times up
entries.text: Every layer's MLP widens the hidden state twice, with a gate projection and an up projection, mixes the two, and narrows it back down. The engine runs both projections as one GEMM, so each token comes out as a single row of 11,264 values: the gate half, then the up half. SwiGLU is the mixing. Output j is silu(gate j) times up j. silu is close to zero for a negative gate and close to the gate itself for a large one, so the gate decides, value by value, how much of up gets through.

entries.title: keep PyTorch's two roundings
entries.text: PyTorch computes this in BF16 as two operations, act_fn(gate) and then the product, so the silu is rounded to BF16 before it meets up. The naive kernel does exactly that, with an accurate expf and a true divide, and reproduces Hugging Face's act tensor bit for bit on every traced layer. This is already a small case of the fusion in chapter 10, "fusion keeps the value on the chip": silu(gate) stays in a register, and the BF16 rounding that writing it out as a tensor would have done is still done there. Every faster version had to keep that chain. Skipping the first rounding looks harmless and gives a different answer: in the example on the right the output moves by one BF16 step.

entries.title: wide loads reach peak bandwidth
entries.text: A thread that loads one value at a time issues a memory instruction for every value it touches. The vector kernel reads a vector of gate values and a vector of up values with two wide loads and writes the matching outputs with one wide store: an eighth of the instructions for the same bytes, so the threads spend their time waiting on memory and not issuing loads. The two loads are half a row apart. The one GEMM writes each row as the gate half and then the up half, so up value j sits half a row after gate value j, and because half a row is a whole number of vectors both loads stay aligned. With enough tokens that is what the kernel is limited by. At the largest size it takes about 360 µs, well under naive's time, which is the GPU's measured peak bandwidth: there is no faster way to move those bytes.

entries.title: at one token, blocks beat wide loads
entries.text: A decode step has one token per request. At one token the row makes only a few hundred vectors, 3 blocks on a GPU with many SMs, and each thread runs its exp and divide chains one after another. The vector kernel was no faster than naive there. So the kernel counts its work first: below half a block per SM, a handful of tokens here, it takes the scalar path, one thread per value, whose blocks spread the same chains over most of the GPU. At one token that is about 3.3 µs, faster than the vector kernel in the same session.

entries.title: a 2D grid stops at 65,535 rows
entries.text: Joe's first draft kept the naive kernel's work split, one thread per output value, on a 2D grid: blocks of threads along a row, and the row on blockIdx.y. It was bit-identical from the start and a little faster than naive at every size, 3.1 µs at one token. The 2D grid had a ceiling: gridDim.y stops at 65,535, so a batch with more rows would not launch. The engine never sends that many rows, but the spec promised any shape, and the tests now launch more rows than that. Both kernels now run on one flat grid and work out the row from the index.

entries.title: 1.6x to 2.1x, but 0.3% of a step
entries.text: At the larger token counts the vector kernel is 1.6x to 2.1x faster than naive, and the bandwidth line shows why the gain stops there. At the smallest token counts the work is small and the launch itself sets the time. Try the token counts on the right. In a decode step SwiGLU is about 0.3% of the kernel time, so none of this moves the token rate. Folding it into the gate/up GEMM's epilogue would be the fusion of chapter 10 again. Writing that row and reading it back is a small share of the gate and up weights the GEMM reads, so at decode it would save a launch more than bytes; that is not done.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: SwiGLU multiplies each up value by a transformed gate. Matching the reference also requires rounding the gate's activation before the product, even though the value now stays in a register. Vector loads reduce memory instructions for the same bytes. Small batches can still run faster with scalar threads because they spread the work across more of the GPU. A faster kernel barely changes decode speed when it takes only a small share of the step. Folding SwiGLU into the gate/up projection would be the fusion of chapter 10 again; at decode it would remove one launch and a row of activations that is tiny next to the weights.

entries.title: one model, cut across GPUs
entries.text: Every chapter so far ran the whole model on one GPU. A model whose weights do not fit in one GPU's memory, or that should read its weights faster than one GPU can, has to be spread over several. Tensor parallelism is one way to do it: every layer's weight matrices are cut into N pieces, and each GPU, called a rank, holds one piece of every layer. For a token, each rank multiplies the token's vector by its own pieces only. What comes out is a partial result: the right size, but only part of the answer. Adding the N partial results gives exactly what the whole matrices would have given. The ranks make that sum, an all-reduce, twice in every layer: after attention and after the MLP. TinyLlama has 22 layers, so one token needs 44 sums. This engine runs on a laptop with one GPU. It cuts TinyLlama the way up to 4 GPUs would need it, loads each rank onto the one GPU and checks the cut there.

entries.title: attention is cut by heads
entries.text: Attention already works in heads. TinyLlama has 32 query heads, and every 8 of them share one of 4 K/V heads. A head never sees another head's numbers until the output projection mixes them. So the cut follows the heads: with N ranks, a rank gets 32/N query heads and 4/N K/V heads, and each group stays together. In the weights a head is a band of rows. The engine keeps Q, K and V in one fused QKV weight, so a rank takes its rows of Q, of K and of V and stores them one after the other. The output projection wo reads the heads along its columns, so the rank takes the same heads' columns of wo, and what wo gives is a partial result of the full width, 2,048 numbers. The heads also set the limit. 4 K/V heads cannot be shared out to more than 4 ranks, so this model can be cut at most 4 ways, and plan_shard_layout() refuses any other count.

entries.title: the MLP is cut by channels
entries.text: The MLP widens a token's 2,048 numbers to 5,632 channels, applies SwiGLU and narrows them back. SwiGLU works one channel at a time: channel c needs only the gate and up values of channel c. So a rank can take 1,408 channels of 5,632 and never need anyone else's. A rank takes its channels' rows of the gate weight and of the up weight, stored together in the fused gate and up weight, and the same channels' columns of wdown. Like wo, wdown then gives a partial result of the full width. The pattern is the same in both halves of the layer: the first matrix is cut by rows, the second by columns, and everything between them happens inside one rank.

entries.title: two sums in every layer
entries.text: Why do the partial results just add? Each number a matrix product writes is a sum: one term for every column of the second matrix. Cut those columns into N groups and each rank adds up one group. The N partial sums together are the whole sum, added in a different order. That works only if each rank has the whole input to its columns, and the row cut gives it exactly that: a rank made the very heads, or channels, whose columns it holds. So the cut costs nothing between the two matrices and one sum at the end of each half, 44 per token. The rest is not cut. RMSNorm needs the whole vector, so its weights are whole in every rank and it runs after the sum. The embedding and the LM head stay whole as well. A unit test adds up the partial outputs of 2 and 4 ranks on a small model and checks they equal the full layer's.

entries.title: a forward pass on the shards
entries.text: With the weights cut, a forward pass on the shards goes like this. Every rank keeps its own K/V cache, for its own K/V heads, and its own scratch buffers. In each layer the shared RMSNorm runs first. Then every rank runs its QKV GEMM, RoPE, its K/V write, attention over its heads and its slice of wo, into a partial result. The all-reduce adds the partial results into the residual stream. The MLP repeats the pattern: the shared RMSNorm, each rank's gate and up GEMM, SwiGLU and wdown, and the second sum. After the last layer the whole LM head turns the vector into logits. On one GPU the ranks run one after another. The pass checks the cut and cannot be faster than the whole model: it does the same work in N smaller pieces. With one rank the logits are the whole model's bit for bit. With 2 and 4 ranks they came within 0.75 of them, and every greedy token was the same (measured). A token took about 8.3 ms with the whole model and about 18 ms with 4 ranks (measured). The ranks take turns on the one GPU, so more ranks is slower here.

entries.title: a rank holds more than its share
entries.text: Cutting the layers divides most of the bytes, not all of them. A rank of 2 holds about 1,200 MiB, 56% of the model and not 50%, and a rank of 4 holds about 710 MiB, 34% and not 25% (measured). The layer matrices do divide by N. The embedding and the LM head are each 32,000 rows of 2,048 numbers, 125.0 MiB, and every rank holds both whole, so 250.0 MiB never shrinks. 2 ranks together hold about 1.1 times the model and 4 ranks about 1.4 times. Counting the bytes of every tensor from the shapes gives the same MiB the engine allocated. In the forward pass here only rank 0 embeds and makes the logits, so the other ranks could drop both tables. They still load them.

entries.title: a column slice is one copy per row
entries.text: Loading a rank means copying its slices out of the file. A slice of rows is one piece of the file, one copy. A slice of columns is not: a matrix is stored row after row, so a rank's columns are a short piece of every row. wo and wdown have 2,048 rows each, and a rank needs 90,269 copies where the whole model needs 201. The first upload_weights gave every copy its own copy into pinned memory, its own transfer and its own event. That cost per copy made a rank load in 4.5 to 5.0 s, about 21 times what the whole model took then, about 220 ms, for a fraction of the bytes (measured at 02e2917). The fix used the order of the copies: the row pieces of one tensor come one after another, and so do their destinations. upload_weights now fills one chunk with all of them and sends it in one call. A rank of 2 loads in about 140 ms and a rank of 4 in about 88 ms, against about 230 ms for the whole model (measured at fdeb8ca).

entries.title: one GPU, and no wire
entries.text: Everything in this chapter ran on one GPU. This laptop has no second device, and the engine has no NCCL, the library that moves data between NVIDIA GPUs. When the ranks share one GPU, a sum is an add in that GPU's memory. On real GPUs each of the 44 sums of a token is a transfer: every rank sends its partial vector, gets the total back, and its next kernel waits for it. What that costs depends on the link between the GPUs, and none of it is measured here. What one GPU can show is the cut: which bytes each rank holds, how long a rank takes to load, and whether the partial results add up to the whole model's. Beyond this engine says what several GPUs would buy.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: Attention is cut by heads and the MLP by channels: rows of the fused QKV and gate and up weights, columns of wo and wdown. TinyLlama's 4 K/V heads allow at most 4 ranks. A rank of 2 holds about 1,200 MiB, 56% of the model and not half (measured): the embedding and the LM head, 125.0 MiB each, stay whole in every rank. A column slice is one copy per row, 90,269 copies against 201; packing the copies of one tensor into one chunk took a rank of 2 from about 4,700 to about 140 ms (measured).

entries.title: where a token's time goes
entries.text: Every chapter changed one kernel and then asked the same question: did the step get shorter? The answer comes from a step profile. Nsight Systems records when each kernel of a decode step starts and ends on the GPU, and a script follows every kernel back to the operation that launched it: the QKV projection, RoPE, attention and so on, through all 22 layers. A profile gives three lengths for one step. The span runs from the start of the first kernel to the end of the last. The busy time is the part of the span in which a kernel was running. The rest of the span is launch gaps, a few microseconds before each kernel. Time per op splits the kernel time by operation. The time a user waits for a token is longer than the span. Between two steps the host schedules, builds the batch, samples and reads the token back. So the kernels add up to less than the step, and the step to less than the token: about 6,400 µs busy, about 7,600 µs of span and about 8.7 ms per token in the same run. One caution. This laptop GPU's clocks move between runs, so two profiles taken weeks apart can differ by more than a small kernel saved. Compare shares inside one profile, and trust a change between profiles only where it is larger than that.

entries.title: every kernel shrank its slice, and the GEMMs kept the step
entries.text: The first profile of a batch-1 decode step, on Oct 15, had 267 kernels in a span of about 8,700 µs. The projections and the LM head, all cuBLAS, took about 6,500 µs of kernel time, attention about 870 µs, and the norms, adds, RoPE, SwiGLU and the cache write about 330 µs together. Then the chapters landed. Fusing each add with the norm after it took 43 launches out of the step. Attention v2 took attention from about 880 to about 270 µs, the largest single cut. Tuning add + RMSNorm took the small kernels from about 280 to about 200 µs. CUDA Graphs removed the gaps: about 1,200 µs of idle time in a step became 88 µs. The GEMMs did not move, because no chapter changed them: about 6,500 µs then and about 6,100 µs now, a difference the clocks explain. Their share of the kernel time rose from 84% to 94% only because everything around them shrank. Sampling is outside the span: one greedy sample kernel after each step, 7.1 µs. One capture reads oddly: on Oct 20 the gaps were about 24% of the span, where today's are about 15%. Gaps depend on what else the machine is doing. Kernel time is the steadier number.

entries.title: most of a token is the read of the weights
entries.text: Foundations gave the floor. A decoded token reads every weight once, about 2.1 GB, and this GPU's memory delivers about 320 GB/s at best, so a token cannot take less than about 6.4 ms. No kernel changes that number. Today's token takes about 6.9 ms with the step replayed from a graph. 93% of it is that read at the peak rate. The kernels are busy for 0.047 ms less than the floor, so they read a little faster than the measured peak, the launch gaps about 0.088 ms, and about 0.46 ms, 7%, pass between the end of one step and the start of the next. So for one request at a time, a faster kernel has nothing left to win. The larger gains in this book came from sharing the read: with 16 rows in a step the same about 2.1 GB serve 16 tokens, and the engine makes 12.0 times the tokens per second it makes alone.

entries.title: the first token of a long prompt was the slow part
entries.text: Decode started close to its floor: the first profiled token already spent 68% of its time on the read of the weights. Prefill was far from it. One 2,048-token prompt took about 1,200 ms to its first token, against about 190 ms for llama.cpp, because every prompt token ran through the decode attention kernel and walked its whole context alone. The cost per prompt token climbed from about 0.13 to 0.58 ms as the prompt grew. The first FlashAttention kernel read the keys from a nearer place and kept the walk: about 1,600 ms, 9% slower. The tiled kernel gives one warp 16 query rows and passes the keys by them 16 at a time on the tensor cores: about 160 ms, 7.2 times less and 12% under llama.cpp in the same session. Its cost per token stays between 0.074 and 0.086 ms at every length measured. What a prefill is made of changed with it. In a profile of the same prompt, attention is about 36 of about 190 ms, 19%, and the 88 GEMMs are 77%. Prefill now looks like decode: mostly cuBLAS. The two systems are not timed in quite the same way, since llama.cpp's number has no sampler in it.

entries.title: under load, vLLM still serves more
entries.text: Under load, requests arrive at random at a set rate, and what counts is goodput: the requests per second that got their first token within 500 ms and every later token within 50 ms on average. The sweep shown here was measured on 2026-11-11 at commit 1feaba9, with the tiled prefill kernel of the FlashAttention prefill chapter. The engine's best goodput is about 4.5 requests per second, at an offered 5. vLLM's is about 7.5 at an offered 8, the highest rate offered, so its real peak was not found. The best goodput of vLLM is 1.6 times the engine's. The tail shows it first. At an offered 5 the engine's TTFT p99 is about 920 ms and vLLM's 63 ms. The engine keeps that p99 inside the SLO up to an offered 4, vLLM up to an offered 6. Inside an answer, the longest wait between two tokens at that rate is about 110 ms with whole prompts and 41 ms with a token budget; vLLM's gaps were not recorded. The comparison is uneven in both directions. vLLM's times include its HTTP server and the engine's do not. Both were held to 16 sequences at once, which is not vLLM's default. The lengths are uniform and the tokens random, not a real chat workload.

entries.title: three things to do next
entries.text: First, serve more than 16 sequences at once. With every request submitted together the engine goes from about 1,400 to about 2,800 tokens per second between 16 and 64 rows, and the KV cache is not what stops it. That run has not been made under load, or against vLLM at its own default. Second, read K and V once per KV head. At 64 rows attention is 44% of the step and grows in proportion to the rows: each row reads its own keys and values, and the 8 query heads that share a KV head each read them again. The prefill kernel does the same: it asks the caches for about 3,300 MB per layer to use about 2.1 MB, with its tensor cores at about 20% of their peak. Third, prepare the next step while this one runs. About 0.46 ms of every batch-1 token, 7%, pass between two steps. Without them a token would sit at 99% of the bandwidth roof where it sits at 93% (calculated). Two smaller ones were left out: a token budget of 256 still costs a lone long prompt 14%, and float Gumbel noise would cut a sampled draw from about 430 µs to under 96 µs but changes the tokens of a fixed seed. None of the three reads fewer bytes. That is the other way past the floor, and beyond this engine is about it.

entries.title: on an H100 SXM, Llama 3 8B's floor is 4.48 ms a token
entries.text: Carry the floor to a model and a GPU people serve: Llama 3 8B in BF16 on an H100 SXM. A decode step reads every weight but the embedding table, about 15 GB, and the H100 SXM's memory is published at 3.35 TB/s, so a token cannot take less than about 4.5 ms. Here the floor is about 6.4 ms: a model that reads about 7.3 times the bytes, on memory about 10 times as fast, still waits on the same division. What the rest of a token would cost there is not known. Here everything above the floor, the kernels, the launch gaps and the time between steps, adds up to about 0.5 ms. If the kernels on the H100 SXM also reached the floor and that part stayed the same, the floor would be about 90% of a token against 93% here: a fixed cost weighs more as the read gets shorter. That is an assumption, not a measurement. These numbers are calculated from published specs. The H100 SXM has no measured step to compare: nothing in this book ran on one or with Llama 3 8B. What carries over is the order of the work: divide the bytes by the bandwidth first, then measure what is left.

entries.title: what to remember
entries.text: A batch-1 token takes about 6.9 ms and 93% of it is the read of about 2.1 GB of weights at the measured peak (calculated from measured values). The GEMMs took about 6,500 µs of the first profile and about 6,100 µs of today's: no chapter changed them. The large wins were outside batch-1 decode: sharing the read across a batch, and prefill, where one 2,048-token prompt went from about 1,200 to about 160 ms to its first token (measured). Under load on 2026-11-11 (commit 1feaba9): the best goodput of vLLM is 1.6 times the engine's, with both systems held to 16 sequences (measured).
